uni-mcom-advanced-cost-accounting.title: M.Com · Advanced Cost Accounting
uni-mcom-advanced-cost-accounting.description: Marginal costing and decisions, standard costing and variance analysis, ABC and strategic cost management, process and joint-product costing, and transfer pricing with solved numericals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian M.Com programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Marginal Costing, CVP and Decision Making
courses.summary: Marginal vs absorption costing and profit reconciliation, cost–volume–profit analysis (P/V ratio, break-even, margin of safety), and short-run decisions: make or buy, key factor, special orders and shutdown.
outcomes: Prepare profit statements under marginal and absorption costing and reconcile them
Compute P/V ratio, break-even point, margin of safety and sales for target profit
Decide make-or-buy and special-order questions using relevant costs
Rank products under a limiting factor
Evaluate temporary shutdown versus continuing operations

scenes.text: A Coimbatore pump maker produced 10,000 pumps but sold 8,000. The cost accountant reports one profit; the finance team another.
The gap is the fixed overhead carried in closing stock.

steps.title: The difference
steps.body: Marginal (variable) costing charges only variable costs to products; fixed costs are period costs written off in full. Absorption costing charges both variable and fixed production overheads to products, so part of fixed overhead is carried forward in closing inventory. Marginal costing statement: Sales − Variable cost = Contribution − Fixed cost = Profit.

steps.title: Reconciliation rule
steps.body: Absorption profit − Marginal profit = (Closing stock units − Opening stock units) × Fixed production overhead per unit (assuming the same rate). Production > sales → absorption profit higher; production < sales → marginal profit higher; equal → same profit.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Production 10,000 units; sales 8,000 at ₹100; variable cost ₹60/unit; fixed production overhead ₹1,00,000 (normal capacity 10,000 → ₹10/unit). No opening stock.
Marginal: contribution 8,000 × 40 = 3,20,000 − 1,00,000 = ₹2,20,000.
Absorption: cost of sales 8,000 × 70 = 5,60,000; profit = 8,00,000 − 5,60,000 = ₹2,40,000.
Difference ₹20,000 = 2,000 units × ₹10.

steps.title: Why managers like marginal costing
steps.body: Profit moves with sales, not production, so managers cannot raise reported profit merely by building stock. Contribution is the basis of CVP and decisions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Including fixed selling overheads in inventory under absorption costing — only production overheads are absorbed. Also, under/over-absorption must be adjusted when actual output differs from normal capacity.

activity.prompt: No opening stock; production 12,000; sales 10,000; fixed production overhead ₹1,80,000 (absorbed on production). By how much does absorption profit exceed marginal profit (₹)?

quiz.q: Under marginal costing, fixed production overhead is:
options: Charged in full to the period
quiz.why: Marginal costing treats fixed costs as period costs, written off against contribution in the period incurred.

quiz.q: When sales exceed production, profit is higher under:
quiz.why: Inventory falls, so absorption costing releases fixed overhead from opening stock into cost of sales, lowering its profit.

quiz.q: Closing stock rises by 500 units; FOH rate ₹12. Difference in profits:
quiz.why: 500 × ₹12 = ₹6,000, with absorption profit higher.

quiz.q: Contribution equals:
quiz.why: Contribution is what remains from sales after variable costs to cover fixed costs and profit.

scenes.text: A school-bag maker sells at ₹100 with variable cost ₹60 and fixed costs of ₹2 lakh a year.
Every bag contributes ₹40 — so 5,000 bags cover fixed costs.

steps.title: Key formulas
steps.body: P/V ratio = Contribution/Sales × 100 = ΔProfit/ΔSales × 100. BEP (units) = Fixed cost/Contribution per unit. BEP (₹) = Fixed cost/P/V ratio. Sales for target profit = (Fixed cost + Target profit)/P/V ratio. Margin of safety (MOS) = Actual sales − BEP sales = Profit/P/V ratio.

steps.title: Break-even chart and assumptions
steps.body: Draw total cost and sales lines; they intersect at BEP; the angle of incidence between them reflects profitability. Assumptions: costs separable into fixed and variable; linear behaviour; constant SP; single product or constant mix; no inventory change. Multi-product: use weighted P/V ratio.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Dividing fixed costs by the P/V ratio to get units — that gives rupees; divide by contribution per unit for units.

activity.prompt: SP ₹50; VC ₹30; FC ₹1,20,000. Units needed to earn a profit of ₹60,000?

quiz.q: P/V ratio 25%; FC ₹1,50,000. BEP sales:
Profit ₹60,000; P/V 30%. MOS:
An increase in selling price, other things equal:
quiz.why: Higher contribution per unit means fewer units are needed to cover fixed costs.

quiz.q: CVP analysis assumes:
options: Constant selling price and linear costs
quiz.why: The standard model assumes linear revenue and cost functions within the relevant range.

lessons.title: Make or Buy, Special Orders and Shutdown

scenes.text: A buyer offers ₹70 per unit for 2,000 extra units. Full cost is ₹80. The sales head wants to refuse.
With spare capacity, only variable cost (₹60) is relevant — the order adds ₹20,000 profit.

steps.title: Relevant costing
steps.body: Relevant costs are future, incremental cash costs that differ between alternatives. Sunk costs and committed fixed costs are irrelevant; opportunity costs and avoidable fixed costs are relevant.

steps.title: Worked example: special order
steps.body: Spare capacity exists. Price ₹70; VC ₹60. Extra contribution = 2,000 × 10 = ₹20,000 → accept, provided it does not disturb regular prices and no extra fixed costs arise. If a special die costing ₹25,000 is needed, the order loses ₹5,000 → reject.

steps.title: Worked example: make or buy
steps.body: Component: material ₹25, labour ₹12, variable overhead ₹8, apportioned fixed overhead ₹10 → total ₹55. Supplier quotes ₹50. Relevant cost of making = ₹45 (fixed overhead unavoidable). Make: saves ₹5 per unit. If the freed capacity could earn contribution of ₹30,000 on 4,000 units (₹7.50 per unit), buying becomes better: 45 + 7.50 = ₹52.50 > ₹50.

steps.title: Shutdown decision
steps.body: Shut down temporarily if contribution < (fixed costs avoidable by shutting) — i.e. compare the loss of operating with the loss of shutdown. Shutdown point (units) = (Total FC − Shutdown FC)/Contribution per unit. Example: FC ₹3,00,000; FC if shut ₹1,20,000; contribution ₹15/unit → shutdown point = 1,80,000/15 = 12,000 units.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using full cost (including apportioned fixed overhead) in make-or-buy or special-order decisions.

activity.prompt: 4,000 units needed. Variable cost to make ₹45; bought-in price ₹50; fixed costs unavoidable; no alternative use of capacity. Saving from making instead of buying (₹)?

quiz.q: Which cost is irrelevant to a decision?
quiz.why: Sunk costs are already incurred and cannot be changed by any choice.

quiz.q: A special order should be accepted at a price above:
options: Variable cost plus any extra specific costs
quiz.why: With spare capacity, any price above incremental cost increases total profit.

quiz.q: Total FC ₹2,00,000; FC if shut ₹80,000; contribution ₹12/unit. Shutdown point:
Opportunity cost is:
options: The benefit forgone from the next best alternative
quiz.why: It measures what is sacrificed by choosing one option, so it is relevant.

scenes.text: Only 6,000 machine hours are available. Product A earns ₹30 contribution per unit, B ₹24.
A needs 3 hours, B only 2 — so B earns more per hour and comes first.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: When one resource limits output, rank products by contribution per unit of the key factor (₹ per machine hour, per kg of material, per labour hour). Produce in that order up to demand, until the resource runs out. Without a constraint, rank by contribution per unit or P/V ratio.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
A: contribution ₹30, 3 hours → ₹10/hour; max demand 1,500 units. B: contribution ₹24, 2 hours → ₹12/hour; max demand 2,000 units. Hours available 6,000.
Step 1: B first: 2,000 × 2 = 4,000 hours; contribution ₹48,000.
Step 2: A with the remaining 2,000 hours: 2,000/3 = 666 full units (2 hours unused); contribution ₹19,980.
Total contribution = ₹67,980.

steps.title: Sales mix decisions
steps.body: To choose between mixes, compute total contribution of each mix less fixed costs. Weighted P/V ratio = total contribution/total sales; composite BEP = FC/weighted P/V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Ranking by contribution per unit when a key factor exists, or ignoring maximum demand limits.

activity.prompt: Material is the key factor (kg limited). Rank by contribution per kg.

quiz.q: Under a key factor, products are ranked by:
options: Contribution per unit of the key factor
quiz.why: The scarce resource should earn the maximum contribution per unit used.

quiz.q: Weighted P/V 30%; FC ₹90,000. Composite BEP:
If no constraint exists, the best product is the one with the highest:
options: Contribution per unit (or P/V ratio given sales limits)
quiz.why: Without a scarce resource, each unit sold adds its contribution, so higher contribution is preferred.

Which statement about marginal costing is correct?
options: Contribution excludes variable cost only for services
Profit varies with sales, not production
It is required for statutory accounts

courses.title: Unit 2 · Standard Costing, Variance Analysis and Budgetary Control
courses.summary: Setting standards; material (price, usage, mix, yield), labour (rate, idle time, efficiency), variable and fixed overhead (expenditure, efficiency, capacity, volume) and sales variances; flexible budgets and budgetary control.
outcomes: Compute and interpret material price, usage and mix variances
Compute labour rate, idle-time and efficiency variances
Analyse variable and fixed overhead variances
Compute sales price and volume variances
Prepare a flexible budget and explain budgetary control

scenes.text: The purchase manager bought steel at ₹19 instead of ₹20 per kg. Production used 50 kg extra.
A favourable price variance, an adverse usage variance — were they linked?

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Material cost variance (MCV) = SQ × SP − AQ × AP. Price variance (MPV) = AQ × (SP − AP). Usage variance (MUV) = SP × (SQ − AQ). MCV = MPV + MUV. SQ = standard quantity for actual output. Usage splits into Mix variance = SP × (RSQ − AQ) and Yield variance = SP × (SQ − RSQ), where RSQ = actual total input in standard proportions. Positive = Favourable (F); negative = Adverse (A).

steps.title: Worked example: mix
steps.body:
Standard mix A 60% at ₹10, B 40% at ₹5. Actual input 100 kg: A 70 kg, B 30 kg. RSQ: A 60, B 40.
Mix variance: A = 10 × (60 − 70) = ₹100 A; B = 5 × (40 − 30) = ₹50 F. Net = ₹50 A (more of the dearer material used).

steps.title: Responsibility
steps.body: Price variance → purchase department (market prices, discounts, quality). Usage variance → production (wastage, pilferage, poor machines, inferior material). A favourable price variance from inferior material can cause an adverse usage variance — investigate together.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using budgeted output instead of actual output to compute SQ, or computing price variance on quantity used when it should be on quantity purchased (if stated at purchase point).

activity.prompt: SQ for actual output 2,000 kg at ₹15; actual 1,900 kg at ₹16. Material usage variance (₹, favourable as positive)?

quiz.q: MPV = AQ × (SP − AP). If AP > SP the variance is:
quiz.why: Paying more than standard increases cost, giving an adverse price variance.

quiz.q: SQ 500 kg, AQ 520 kg, SP ₹10. MUV:
quiz.why: 10 × (500 − 520) = −₹200, an adverse usage variance.

quiz.q: The usage variance can be split into:
quiz.why: Usage reflects both the proportions of materials (mix) and output from total input (yield).

quiz.q: Responsibility for material price variance usually lies with:
quiz.why: Purchase managers control supplier selection and price.

scenes.text: A three-hour power failure left 100 paid hours idle in the assembly shop.
Idle time is shown separately so that workers are not blamed for inefficiency.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Labour cost variance = SH × SR − AH(paid) × AR. Rate variance = AH(paid) × (SR − AR). Idle time variance = Idle hours × SR (always adverse). Efficiency variance = SR × (SH − AH worked). Check: Rate + Idle + Efficiency = LCV. SH = standard hours for actual output.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body: Rate: wage revisions, overtime premium, using higher-grade workers. Efficiency: poor supervision, bad material, machine breakdowns, learning effect. Idle time: power failure, waiting for material, strikes (abnormal idle time may be charged to costing P&L).

steps.title: Gang composition (mix)
steps.body: When different grades work together, Labour mix variance = SR × (RSH − AH worked) by grade, where RSH = actual hours worked in standard gang ratio.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Computing efficiency on hours paid instead of hours worked, which hides idle time inside efficiency.

activity.prompt: SH for actual output 500 at ₹20; actual hours worked 520 (no idle time). Labour efficiency variance, magnitude in ₹ (it is adverse)?

quiz.q: Idle time variance is always:
quiz.why: Idle hours are paid but produce nothing, so they always add cost.

quiz.q: Hours paid 1,000 at ₹12; SR ₹10. Rate variance:
Labour efficiency is computed on:
quiz.why: Only hours actually worked reflect productivity; idle hours are separated.

quiz.q: A likely cause of adverse efficiency variance:
quiz.why: Bad material slows work and increases rejections, raising hours per unit.

scenes.text: The factory planned 12,000 units but made 11,000. Fixed overhead stayed almost the same.
Less output absorbed less overhead — a volume variance.

steps.title: Fixed overhead formulas
steps.body: FOH cost variance = Absorbed FOH − Actual FOH, where Absorbed = Actual output × Standard FOH rate per unit (or SH × rate per hour). Expenditure (budget) variance = Budgeted FOH − Actual FOH. Volume variance = Absorbed − Budgeted FOH. Volume splits into Efficiency = Rate/hr × (SH − AH) and Capacity = Rate/hr × (AH − Budgeted hours). (Calendar variance arises if working days differ.)

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: Expenditure variances are controllable by department heads. Volume variances reflect capacity use and are often due to demand or breakdowns; they do not represent cash wasted but under-recovery of fixed costs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using budgeted output to compute absorbed overhead, or reporting a variable overhead volume variance (none exists, as variable overhead flexes with output).

activity.prompt: Budgeted FOH ₹2,00,000 for 10,000 units; actual output 10,500 units; actual FOH ₹2,04,000. FOH volume variance (₹, favourable positive)?

quiz.q: FOH expenditure variance =
quiz.why: It compares what was budgeted to be spent with what was actually spent.

quiz.q: Volume variance is favourable when:
quiz.why: Producing more than budget absorbs more fixed overhead than budgeted.

quiz.q: Capacity variance arises from:
options: Working more or fewer hours than budgeted
quiz.why: It values the difference between actual and budgeted hours at the fixed rate per hour.

quiz.q: Variable overhead has no:
quiz.why: Variable overhead is flexed with output, so there is no under-recovery from volume changes.

story.title: Sold more, earned less per unit

scenes.text: The sales team cut the price by ₹5 and sold 100 units more than budget.
Sales value rose, but how much came from price and how much from volume?

steps.title: Sales value variances
steps.body: Sales value variance = Actual sales − Budgeted sales. Price variance = AQ × (AP − BP). Volume variance = BP × (AQ − BQ). Volume may be split into mix and quantity variances for multiple products. Sales margin variances use standard profit or contribution instead of price.

steps.title: Flexible budget
steps.body: A flexible budget recognises cost behaviour and shows costs for different activity levels: Total cost = Fixed + Variable per unit × units (semi-variable costs split). Comparing actual cost with the flexed budget for the actual level gives meaningful variances, unlike comparing with a fixed budget.

steps.title: Worked example: flexed cost
steps.body: Fixed ₹50,000; variable ₹6 per unit; semi-variable ₹20,000 at 5,000 units and ₹26,000 at 8,000 units (variable part ₹2/unit, fixed ₹10,000). Cost at 8,000 units = 50,000 + 48,000 + 26,000 = ₹1,24,000.

steps.title: Budgetary control steps
steps.body: Set budgets (sales budget usually first, limited by the principal budget factor), record actuals, compare, analyse variances, take corrective action, and revise. Zero-based budgeting justifies every expense afresh; performance budgeting links spending to outputs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Comparing actual costs at 8,000 units with a fixed budget prepared for 10,000 units and calling the difference 'savings'.

activity.prompt: Budget 2,000 units at ₹40; actual 1,800 units at ₹42. Sales price variance (₹, favourable positive)?

quiz.q: Sales volume variance uses:
quiz.why: Volume variance isolates the quantity effect by valuing it at budgeted price.

quiz.q: A flexible budget is prepared for:
quiz.why: It adjusts costs to the actual level of activity, enabling fair comparison.

quiz.why: Change ₹6,000 ÷ 3,000 units = ₹2 per unit.

quiz.q: The principal budget factor is:

quiz.why: Budgets start from the binding constraint; usually that is sales demand.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Activity-Based Costing and Strategic Cost Management
courses.summary: Activity-based costing and cost drivers, target and life-cycle costing, JIT and throughput accounting, cost of quality, Kaizen and value-chain analysis.
outcomes: Allocate overheads using activity cost pools and drivers and compare with traditional absorption
Compute target cost and the cost gap; explain life-cycle costing
Compute throughput accounting ratio and rank products on a bottleneck
Classify costs of quality and explain Kaizen and value-chain analysis

story.title: The low-volume product that looked profitable

scenes.text: A cosmetics plant makes a mass-market cream (X) and a small-batch premium serum (Y).
Machine-hour absorption says Y is cheap. ABC shows Y consumes most of the setups and inspections.

steps.title: Steps in ABC
steps.body: 1. Identify major activities (setups, material ordering, inspection, machine running, dispatch). 2. Pool overhead costs by activity. 3. Choose a cost driver for each pool (number of setups, orders, inspections, machine hours). 4. Compute the cost driver rate = pool cost ÷ total driver volume. 5. Charge products: driver rate × driver units used. Cost hierarchy: unit-level, batch-level, product-sustaining, facility-sustaining.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Setup cost ₹1,20,000 for 60 setups → ₹2,000/setup. Inspection ₹80,000 for 400 inspections → ₹200 each.
X: 10,000 units, 10 setups, 100 inspections → 20,000 + 20,000 = ₹40,000 → ₹4/unit.
Y: 1,000 units, 50 setups, 300 inspections → 1,00,000 + 60,000 = ₹1,60,000 → ₹160/unit.

steps.title: Traditional comparison
steps.body: Same ₹2,00,000 absorbed on machine hours: X 18,000 hours, Y 2,000 hours → ₹10 per hour. X gets ₹1,80,000 (₹18/unit); Y gets ₹20,000 (₹20/unit). Traditional costing overcosts the high-volume X and undercosts the complex low-volume Y — cross-subsidisation.

steps.title: When ABC helps most
steps.body: High overheads relative to direct costs, diverse products, batch sizes that vary widely, and overheads driven by complexity rather than volume. Activity-based management (ABM) then targets non-value-adding activities.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Dividing batch-level costs by units before multiplying by batches used — always charge by driver volume first, then divide by units.

activity.prompt: Material-ordering pool rate is ₹500 per order. A product needs 30 orders for 6,000 units. Ordering cost per unit (₹)?

quiz.q: A cost driver is:
options: The factor that causes an activity's cost to change
quiz.why: Cost drivers link activity cost to the products that consume the activity.

quiz.q: Machine setup cost is a:
quiz.why: Setup is incurred once per batch regardless of the number of units in the batch.

quiz.q: Traditional volume-based absorption tends to:
quiz.why: Volume drivers spread batch costs over many units of high-volume products, so complex low-volume products get too little.

quiz.q: Inspection pool ₹50,000; 250 inspections. Driver rate:
quiz.why: 50,000 ÷ 250 = ₹200 per inspection.

scenes.text: Market research says a new smart speaker will sell at ₹1,200. The company wants a 25% margin on price.
So the cost must not exceed ₹900 — designers must close the gap.

steps.title: Target costing
steps.body: Target cost = Target selling price − Target profit. Cost gap = Estimated current cost − Target cost. Close the gap through value engineering (removing features customers don't value), design for manufacture, supplier collaboration, and component standardisation. It is applied mainly at the design stage, where most costs are committed.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Target price ₹1,200; margin 25% of price → target profit ₹300; target cost ₹900. Current design cost ₹1,000 → cost gap ₹100 (10% reduction needed).

steps.title: Life-cycle costing
steps.body: Tracks all costs of a product over its life: R&D and design, launch, production, marketing, after-sales service and disposal. Life-cycle profit = total life-cycle revenue − total life-cycle costs. It shows that pre-production costs can be large and that products must recover them over their life.

steps.title: Worked example: life-cycle cost per unit
steps.body: R&D ₹40 lakh; design ₹10 lakh; production ₹150 lakh for 1,00,000 units; marketing ₹30 lakh; disposal ₹5 lakh. Total ₹235 lakh → ₹235 per unit. A price based only on production cost (₹150) would lose money.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Computing target cost as cost plus margin — target costing starts from the market price and works backwards.

activity.prompt: Target price ₹2,500; required profit 20% of price; estimated cost ₹2,150. Cost gap (₹)?

quiz.q: Target cost equals:
quiz.why: Target costing works backward from the price customers will pay.

quiz.q: Value engineering aims to:
options: Reduce cost without reducing value to customers
quiz.why: It removes or redesigns elements that cost more than the value they deliver.

quiz.q: Most of a product's costs are committed at the:
quiz.why: Design choices fix materials, processes and features, locking in most later costs.

quiz.q: Life-cycle costing includes:
quiz.why: It accumulates every cost over the product's entire life.

scenes.text: A bakery can mix and pack plenty, but its single oven runs 24 hours a day.
Every product should be judged by what it earns per oven hour.

steps.title: Just-in-time
steps.body: JIT purchasing and production pull materials only when needed, aiming at zero inventory, zero defects and short lead times. Requires reliable suppliers, quality at source, flexible workforce and small batches. Backflush costing suits JIT: costs are recorded at completion or sale using standard costs, skipping detailed WIP tracking.

steps.title: Throughput accounting
steps.body: Based on Goldratt's theory of constraints. Throughput = Sales − Direct material (all other costs treated as fixed 'total factory cost'). Return per factory hour = (Price − Material) ÷ Bottleneck hours per unit. Cost per factory hour = Total factory cost ÷ Total bottleneck hours available. TA ratio = Return per factory hour ÷ Cost per factory hour; > 1 means the product is profitable.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Price ₹100; material ₹40; bottleneck time 6 minutes (0.1 hour). Return per hour = 60/0.1 = ₹600. Total factory cost ₹4,80,000; bottleneck hours 1,200 → ₹400 per hour. TA ratio = 600/400 = 1.5.

steps.title: Improving the ratio
steps.body: Raise price, cut material cost, reduce time on the bottleneck, or elevate the constraint (add capacity). Building stock at non-bottleneck stations does not raise throughput.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating labour as a variable cost in throughput accounting — only direct material is variable.

activity.prompt: Price ₹250; material ₹100; bottleneck time 15 minutes; cost per factory hour ₹450. TA ratio?

quiz.q: Throughput in TA is:
quiz.why: Throughput accounting treats only material as truly variable in the short run.

quiz.q: A TA ratio below 1 means:
options: The product earns more than factory cost per hour
The product does not cover factory cost per bottleneck hour
quiz.why: Return per bottleneck hour is less than the cost of running the factory per hour.

quiz.q: Backflush costing suits:
quiz.why: With little WIP, detailed tracking adds little value, so costs are flushed at completion.

quiz.q: Theory of constraints says throughput is limited by:
quiz.why: The slowest resource determines system output.

lessons.title: Cost of Quality, Kaizen and Value Chain

scenes.text: A car maker recalls 20,000 vehicles for a faulty part costing ₹200 to fix at the plant.
In the field, each fix costs ₹5,000 plus reputation — external failure is the dearest quality cost.

steps.title: Four categories
steps.body: Prevention costs: quality planning, training, supplier evaluation, preventive maintenance. Appraisal costs: inspection, testing, quality audits. Internal failure costs (before delivery): scrap, rework, downtime, re-inspection. External failure costs (after delivery): warranty claims, returns, recalls, lost goodwill. Conformance = prevention + appraisal; non-conformance = failures. TQM argues more prevention lowers total cost.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Training ₹2 lakh; inspection ₹3 lakh; rework ₹4 lakh; warranty ₹6 lakh; scrap ₹1 lakh. Prevention ₹2 lakh; appraisal ₹3 lakh; internal failure ₹5 lakh; external failure ₹6 lakh; total ₹16 lakh, of which non-conformance ₹11 lakh (69%).

steps.title: Kaizen costing
steps.body: Continuous small improvements during the production phase, with periodic cost-reduction targets, as opposed to target costing at design stage. Employees suggest improvements; standards are tightened steadily.

steps.title: Value chain
steps.body: Porter's value chain: primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service) and support activities (firm infrastructure, HR, technology development, procurement). lessons.title: Process Losses: Normal, Abnormal Loss and Gain

scenes.text: A chemical plant expects 10% of input to evaporate. This month it lost 13%.
The expected 10% is absorbed by good units; the extra 3% is abnormal and charged to costing P&L.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: Normal loss: expected, unavoidable; its scrap value is credited to the process; its cost is borne by good output. Abnormal loss: loss above normal; valued at the same cost per unit as good output and transferred to Abnormal Loss A/c (then to costing P&L after crediting scrap). Abnormal gain: actual loss below normal; valued at normal cost per unit and debited to the process. Cost per unit = (Total cost − Scrap value of normal loss) ÷ (Input − Normal loss units).

steps.title: Worked example: abnormal loss
steps.body:
Input 1,000 units at ₹40 = ₹40,000; labour and overheads ₹14,500; total ₹54,500. Normal loss 10% (100 units), scrap ₹5 each = ₹500. Output 870 units.
Cost per unit = (54,500 − 500)/900 = ₹60.
Abnormal loss = 900 − 870 = 30 units × 60 = ₹1,800.
Output transferred = 870 × 60 = ₹52,200.
Check: 52,200 + 1,800 + 500 = ₹54,500.

steps.title: Worked example: abnormal gain
steps.body: Same data, output 920 units. Abnormal gain = 920 − 900 = 20 units × 60 = ₹1,200 (debited to process). Output = 920 × 60 = ₹55,200. In the Abnormal Gain A/c, the scrap value lost on the 20 units (₹100) is debited, so net gain to costing P&L = ₹1,100.

steps.title: Account structure
steps.body: Process A/c Dr side: materials, labour, overheads, abnormal gain. Cr side: normal loss (scrap), abnormal loss, output transferred to next process or finished stock.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Dividing total cost by actual output (which hides the abnormal loss), or valuing abnormal loss at scrap value instead of full cost.

lessons.title: Equivalent Production: FIFO and Weighted Average

scenes.text: At month-end 2,000 tins of paint are filled with material but only half mixed.

steps.title: Equivalent units
steps.body: Equivalent units (EU) = Physical units × Degree of completion, computed separately for each cost element (material, labour, overheads). Under FIFO, opening WIP is completed first: EU = Opening WIP × work remaining + Units started and completed + Closing WIP × completion. Under weighted average, opening WIP costs are added to current costs and EU = Units completed + Closing WIP × completion.

steps.title: Worked example: FIFO
steps.body:
Opening WIP 1,000 units (material 100%, conversion 60%), cost ₹15,000. Started 9,000. Completed 8,000. Closing WIP 2,000 (material 100%, conversion 50%). Current costs: material ₹90,000; conversion ₹1,26,000.
EU material: 0 + 7,000 + 2,000 = 9,000 → ₹10.
EU conversion: 400 + 7,000 + 1,000 = 8,400 → ₹15.
Closing WIP = 2,000 × 10 + 1,000 × 15 = ₹35,000.
Completed = 15,000 + 400 × 15 + 7,000 × 25 = 15,000 + 6,000 + 1,75,000 = ₹1,96,000.
Check: 1,96,000 + 35,000 = ₹2,31,000 = total cost.

steps.title: Weighted average version
steps.body: Using the same data with opening WIP cost split as material ₹10,000 and conversion ₹5,000: EU material = 8,000 + 2,000 = 10,000; cost (10,000 + 90,000)/10,000 = ₹10. EU conversion = 8,000 + 1,000 = 9,000; cost (5,000 + 1,26,000)/9,000 = ₹14.556. The two methods differ when cost per unit changes between periods.

steps.title: Losses and EU
steps.body: Normal loss units get zero EU (cost absorbed by good units); abnormal loss units get EU at their degree of completion.

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Joint products: two or more products of significant value produced simultaneously from the same input up to a split-off point. By-products: products of minor value produced incidentally. Joint costs are costs before split-off; separable costs are after.

steps.title: Worked example: sell or process further

steps.title: By-product accounting

steps.title: Objectives and methods
steps.body: Objectives: goal congruence, performance evaluation, divisional autonomy, and (internationally) tax compliance. Methods: market-based (best when a competitive external market exists); cost-based (variable cost, full cost, cost-plus); negotiated; dual pricing (seller credited at market, buyer charged at cost).

steps.title: General rule
steps.body: Minimum transfer price = Marginal (variable) cost per unit + Opportunity cost per unit (contribution lost on external sales). Maximum = the buying division's net marginal revenue or the external purchase price. With spare capacity, opportunity cost is zero, so min TP = variable cost.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A's variable cost ₹40; external price ₹60. Full capacity: min TP = 40 + 20 = ₹60. Spare capacity: min TP = ₹40. B can buy outside at ₹58 → negotiable range with spare capacity ₹40–58; at full capacity there is no range below ₹60, so B should buy outside (₹58) unless quality or supply reasons apply.

steps.title: Worked example: selling costs saved
steps.body: Variable cost ₹35; external price ₹55; external selling cost ₹3 per unit avoided on internal transfers; no spare capacity. Lost contribution = 55 − 3 − 35 = ₹17. Min TP = 35 + 17 = ₹52.

steps.title: International transfer pricing
steps.body: Cross-border transfers between associated enterprises must follow the arm's length principle under the Income-tax Act (Chapter X) and OECD guidelines; methods include comparable uncontrolled price, resale price, cost plus, profit split and TNMM.

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: Marginal costing
steps.body: P/V = C/S. BEP units = FC/C per unit; BEP ₹ = FC/P/V. Target sales = (FC + profit)/P/V. MOS = profit/P/V. Absorption − marginal profit = Δstock × FOH rate. Shutdown point = (FC − shutdown FC)/C per unit. Key factor: rank by C per unit of the factor.

steps.title: Variances
steps.body: MPV = AQ(SP − AP); MUV = SP(SQ − AQ); Mix = SP(RSQ − AQ); Yield = SP(SQ − RSQ). LRV = AH paid(SR − AR); Idle = idle hrs × SR; LEV = SR(SH − AH worked). FOH: Expenditure = B − A; Volume = Absorbed − B; Efficiency = rate(SH − AH); Capacity = rate(AH − BH). VOH: Expenditure = AH × SR − A; Efficiency = SR(SH − AH). Sales: Price = AQ(AP − BP); Volume = BP(AQ − BQ).

steps.title: ABC, process, joint, TP
steps.body: ABC rate = pool/driver volume. Target cost = price − profit. TA ratio = (P − M)/bottleneck hrs ÷ factory cost per hr. Process: cost per unit = (cost − normal scrap)/(input − normal loss). FIFO EU = opening × remaining + started-completed + closing × %. Joint: physical, sales value, NRV. Min TP = VC + opportunity cost.

scenes.text: A listed Pune auto-parts maker raises funds in London and reports to SEBI in India. Its CFO asks: why can't one set of accounts satisfy both investors?
India chose convergence, not adoption: Ind AS are IFRS-based standards notified by the Central Government with a few carve-outs.

steps.title: What Ind AS are
steps.body: Ind AS are notified under Section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013 through the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015. They are converged with IFRS issued by the IASB, with carve-outs suited to Indian conditions. Companies not covered continue to follow the older Accounting Standards (AS) under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules.

steps.title: Phased roadmap
steps.body: Phase I (from accounting periods beginning 1 April 2016): listed or unlisted companies with net worth of ₹500 crore or more, plus their holding, subsidiary, joint venture and associate companies. Phase II (from 1 April 2017): all listed companies and unlisted companies with net worth of ₹250 crore or more. Once a company applies Ind AS it cannot switch back. Separate roadmaps exist for banks, NBFCs and insurers.

steps.title: Elements of financial statements
steps.body: Asset: a present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events. Liability: a present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events. Equity: residual interest in assets after deducting liabilities. Income: increases in assets or decreases in liabilities that increase equity, other than owner contributions. Expenses: the opposite, other than distributions to owners.

steps.title: Qualitative characteristics
steps.body: Fundamental: relevance (including materiality) and faithful representation (complete, neutral, free from error). Enhancing: comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability. Enhancing characteristics improve useful information but cannot make irrelevant or misrepresented information useful.

steps.title: Measurement bases
steps.body: Historical cost and current value. Current value includes fair value (exit price between market participants, Ind AS 113), value in use for assets / fulfilment value for liabilities, and current cost. The going-concern assumption is the underlying assumption.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Writing 'prudence means understating profits' — the framework treats prudence as caution under uncertainty that supports neutrality, not deliberate understatement. Also, the Conceptual Framework is not itself an Ind AS and does not override any specific standard.

quiz.why: Phase II, from 1 April 2017, covered all listed companies and unlisted companies with net worth of ₹250 crore or more.

quiz.q: Which is a fundamental qualitative characteristic?
quiz.why: Relevance and faithful representation are the two fundamental characteristics; the others only enhance usefulness.

scenes.text: An intern submits a balance sheet, P&L and cash flow to the audit partner. The partner sends it back: 'Where is the statement of changes in equity and the comparative period?'
Ind AS 1 lists exactly what a complete set contains, and Division II of Schedule III gives the format.

steps.title: A complete set
steps.body: (a) Balance sheet at the end of the period; (b) statement of profit and loss for the period, including Other Comprehensive Income (OCI); (c) statement of changes in equity; (d) statement of cash flows (Ind AS 7); (e) notes, including material accounting policy information; (f) comparative information for the preceding period; and (g) a balance sheet at the beginning of the preceding period when a policy is applied retrospectively, items are restated or reclassified with a material effect (the 'third balance sheet').

steps.title: OCI items
steps.body: OCI is split into items that will not be reclassified to profit or loss (remeasurement of defined benefit plans, revaluation surplus, FVOCI equity instruments) and items that may be reclassified (exchange differences on translating foreign operations, effective portion of cash-flow hedges, FVOCI debt instruments). Total comprehensive income = profit + OCI.

steps.title: Current vs non-current
steps.body: An asset is current if it is expected to be realised within the normal operating cycle, held for trading, expected to be realised within 12 months after the reporting period, or is cash not restricted. A liability is current if it is settled in the operating cycle, held for trading, due within 12 months, or the entity has no right at the reporting date to defer settlement for at least 12 months.

steps.title: Worked example: total comprehensive income
steps.body:
Profit after tax ₹80 lakh. Actuarial loss on gratuity ₹6 lakh (tax 25%). Gain on FVOCI equity shares ₹10 lakh (tax 25%). Translation gain on foreign subsidiary ₹4 lakh (no tax).
Step 1: Not reclassified, net of tax: −6 × 0.75 + 10 × 0.75 = −4.5 + 7.5 = ₹3 lakh.
Step 2: May be reclassified: ₹4 lakh.
Step 3: OCI = 3 + 4 = ₹7 lakh. Total comprehensive income = 80 + 7 = ₹87 lakh.

steps.title: Offsetting rule
steps.body: Assets and liabilities, income and expenses are not offset unless an Ind AS requires or permits it — e.g. gains on disposal of PPE are shown net of carrying amount and selling costs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Classifying a term loan as non-current when a covenant breach at the reporting date made it repayable on demand — if the lender has not agreed before the reporting date to a grace period of at least 12 months, the loan is current.

activity.prompt: Profit ₹50 lakh; revaluation surplus on land ₹8 lakh (tax 25%); cash-flow hedge gain ₹2 lakh (tax 25%). Compute total comprehensive income (₹ lakh).

quiz.q: Which item in OCI may be reclassified to profit or loss later?
options: Exchange difference on translating a foreign operation
quiz.why: On disposal of a foreign operation, the accumulated translation reserve is recycled to profit or loss, unlike the other three items.

quiz.q: A third balance sheet is required when:
options: A policy is applied retrospectively with a material effect on the opening balance sheet
quiz.why: Ind AS 1 requires a balance sheet at the beginning of the preceding period when retrospective application, restatement or reclassification materially affects it.

quiz.q: Which is NOT part of a complete set of Ind AS financial statements?
quiz.why: The Board's report is required by the Companies Act but is not one of the financial statements listed in Ind AS 1.

quiz.q: A liability due in 8 months is classified as:
quiz.why: A liability due for settlement within 12 months after the reporting period is current.

lessons.title: Ind AS 8 and Ind AS 10: Policies, Estimates, Errors and Later Events

scenes.text: While closing FY 2025-26, the accountant finds that depreciation of ₹50,000 on a new machine was never booked in FY 2024-25.
It is not a current-year expense. Ind AS 8 says restate the comparatives — a prior-period error.

steps.title: Change in accounting policy
steps.body: Allowed only if required by an Ind AS or if it results in reliable and more relevant information. Applied retrospectively: adjust opening equity of the earliest period presented and restate comparatives as if the policy had always applied, unless impracticable. Example: changing inventory cost formula from FIFO to weighted average.

steps.title: Change in accounting estimate
steps.body: Estimates (useful life, residual value, bad-debt allowance, warranty provision) are revised as new information arrives. Applied prospectively in the current and future periods. Example: a machine costing ₹10 lakh, life 10 years, after 4 years (WDV-free SLM book value ₹6 lakh) is now expected to last 3 more years: new annual depreciation = 6/3 = ₹2 lakh.

steps.title: Worked example: prior-period error
steps.body:
FY 2024-25 depreciation of ₹50,000 omitted; tax rate 25%; discovered in FY 2025-26.
Step 1: Restate FY 2024-25 comparatives: depreciation +50,000, tax expense −12,500, profit −37,500.
Step 2: Machine carrying amount −50,000; deferred tax liability −12,500 (or deferred tax asset).
Step 3: Opening retained earnings of FY 2025-26 reduced by ₹37,500 in the statement of changes in equity.
Step 4: Disclose nature of error and amounts for each line item. The current year P&L is NOT charged.

steps.title: Ind AS 10: events after the reporting period
steps.body: Events between the reporting date and the date the financial statements are approved for issue. Adjusting events give evidence of conditions existing at the reporting date (settlement of a court case, discovery of fraud, a debtor's insolvency revealing an impaired receivable, sale of inventory below cost) — adjust the amounts. Non-adjusting events reflect conditions arising after the date (fire destroying a plant, major acquisition, fall in market value of investments, dividends declared after the date) — disclose if material. Dividends declared after the reporting date are not a liability at that date.

steps.title: Going concern override
steps.body: If after the reporting date management decides to liquidate or has no realistic alternative but to cease trading, statements must not be prepared on a going-concern basis even though the cause arose later.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating a change in useful life as a policy change (it is an estimate — prospective), or booking a prior-period error in the current year's profit and loss.

activity.prompt: Reporting date 31 March 2026; approval 20 May 2026. Classify each event.

items.text: 15 April: major customer declared insolvent; its debt existed on 31 March
10 April: court settles a case pending at 31 March for ₹12 lakh
25 April: year-end inventory sold below cost
12 May: acquisition of a competitor announced

quiz.q: A change from straight-line to a units-of-production depreciation method because the usage pattern changed is treated as:
quiz.why: Ind AS 16 treats a change in depreciation method as a change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively.

quiz.q: Prior-period errors are corrected by:
quiz.why: Ind AS 8 requires retrospective restatement of comparatives and opening balances for material prior-period errors.

quiz.q: Machine book value ₹9 lakh after 3 years; remaining life now revised to 4 years, nil residual value. New annual depreciation:
quiz.why: Revised estimates apply prospectively, so depreciation = carrying amount ÷ remaining life = 9 ÷ 4 = ₹2.25 lakh.

quiz.q: Dividends declared after the reporting period are:
options: Not a liability; disclosed in notes
A liability at the reporting date
Debited to the previous year's P&L
quiz.why: No obligation exists at the reporting date, so Ind AS 10 requires only disclosure.

lessons.title: Ind AS 115: Revenue from Contracts with Customers

scenes.text: A Bengaluru retailer sells a phone with one year of servicing for a bundled ₹36,000.
How much is revenue on day one? Ind AS 115 allocates the price on relative standalone selling prices.

steps.title: The five steps
steps.body: 1. Identify the contract with a customer. 2. Identify the separate performance obligations (distinct goods or services). 3. Determine the transaction price (including variable consideration, significant financing component, non-cash consideration, amounts payable to the customer). 4. Allocate the transaction price to performance obligations in proportion to standalone selling prices. 5. Recognise revenue when (or as) each obligation is satisfied — at a point in time or over time.

steps.title: Worked example: allocation
steps.body:
Bundle price ₹36,000. Standalone prices: phone ₹30,000, service ₹10,000 (total ₹40,000).
Phone: 36,000 × 30/40 = ₹27,000 — recognised at delivery.
Service: 36,000 × 10/40 = ₹9,000 — recognised over 12 months = ₹750 per month.
At the end of month 3: revenue = 27,000 + 3 × 750 = ₹29,250; contract liability = ₹6,750.

steps.title: Over time vs point in time
steps.body: Revenue is recognised over time if (a) the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits (cleaning service), (b) the entity's performance creates or enhances an asset the customer controls (building on customer's land), or (c) the asset has no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for work done. Otherwise, at the point control transfers (indicators: right to payment, legal title, physical possession, risks and rewards, acceptance).

steps.title: Worked example: input method
steps.body: Contract price ₹10 crore; estimated total cost ₹8 crore; cost incurred to date ₹3 crore. Progress = 3/8 = 37.5%. Revenue to date = 10 × 37.5% = ₹3.75 crore; profit recognised = 3.75 − 3 = ₹0.75 crore. If expected total cost rose to ₹11 crore, the expected loss of ₹1 crore is provided immediately under Ind AS 37 (onerous contract).

steps.title: Variable consideration
steps.body: Estimate by the expected-value or most-likely-amount method, but include it only to the extent it is highly probable that a significant reversal will not occur (the constraint).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Allocating a discount entirely to one item, or recognising the full bundle on delivery. Discounts are allocated proportionately unless observable evidence shows they relate to specific obligations.

activity.prompt: Laptop + 2-year warranty extension sold for ₹66,000. Standalone prices: laptop ₹63,000, extension ₹9,000. Revenue allocated to the laptop (₹)?

quiz.q: Step 4 of Ind AS 115 is:
options: Allocate the price to performance obligations
quiz.why: After the price is determined (step 3) it is allocated to obligations on relative standalone selling prices (step 4).

quiz.q: Contract ₹20 crore, total cost ₹16 crore, cost to date ₹4 crore. Revenue to date by input method:
quiz.why: Progress is 4/16 = 25%, and 25% of ₹20 crore gives revenue of ₹5 crore.

quiz.q: The constraint on variable consideration requires inclusion only when:
options: It is highly probable that a significant reversal will not occur
quiz.why: Ind AS 115 limits variable consideration to the amount for which a significant revenue reversal is highly improbable.

quiz.q: A contract liability arises when:
options: The customer pays before the entity performs
quiz.why: Consideration received before performance is an obligation to transfer goods or services, shown as a contract liability.

questions.q: Under Ind AS, the fundamental qualitative characteristics are:
questions.why: The Conceptual Framework names relevance and faithful representation as fundamental.

questions.q: Phase I of Ind AS applied from accounting periods beginning:
questions.why: Phase I companies (net worth ₹500 crore or more) applied Ind AS from 1 April 2016, with comparatives for 2015-16.

questions.q: Remeasurement loss on a defined benefit plan is shown in:
questions.why: Ind AS 19 remeasurements go to OCI and are never recycled to profit or loss.

questions.q: Profit ₹40 lakh; FVOCI equity gain ₹4 lakh and translation loss ₹2 lakh (ignore tax). Total comprehensive income:
questions.why: OCI = 4 − 2 = ₹2 lakh, so total comprehensive income = 40 + 2 = ₹42 lakh.

questions.q: A change in the estimated useful life of an asset is applied:
questions.why: Changes in estimates affect the current and future periods only.

questions.q: Prior-year salary ₹2 lakh omitted, tax 30%. Adjustment to opening retained earnings:
questions.why: The after-tax effect is 2 × (1 − 0.30) = ₹1.4 lakh, which reduces opening retained earnings.

questions.q: A fire destroying a plant after the reporting date but before approval is:
questions.why: The condition (fire) did not exist at the reporting date, so it is non-adjusting.

questions.q: Settlement after year-end of a lawsuit pending at year-end is:
questions.why: It provides evidence about an obligation that existed at the reporting date.

questions.q: Bundle ₹45,000; standalone prices A ₹40,000 and B ₹10,000. Allocation to B:
Revenue is recognised over time when:
options: The customer simultaneously receives and consumes benefits
questions.why: Simultaneous receipt and consumption is one of the three over-time criteria.

questions.q: Contract price ₹12 crore, estimated total cost ₹9 crore, cost to date ₹6 crore. Profit recognised to date:
questions.why: Progress 6/9 = 2/3; revenue = ₹8 crore; profit = 8 − 6 = ₹2 crore.

questions.q: If an expected total contract cost exceeds the contract price, the expected loss is:
questions.why: An onerous contract provision is recognised at once for the whole expected loss.

questions.q: A loan with a covenant breach at year-end, repayable on demand, where the bank grants a waiver only after year-end, is shown as:
questions.why: At the reporting date the entity had no right to defer settlement for 12 months, so the loan is current.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Amalgamation, Business Combinations & Reconstruction
courses.summary: Amalgamation under AS 14 (merger vs purchase), computation of purchase consideration, accounting in the books of the transferee, the acquisition method of Ind AS 103 with goodwill and bargain purchase, and internal reconstruction by capital reduction.
outcomes: Distinguish amalgamation in the nature of merger from purchase under AS 14
Compute purchase consideration by the net payment and net assets methods
Pass entries for pooling of interests and purchase methods
Measure goodwill, NCI and bargain purchase gain under Ind AS 103
Prepare a capital reduction scheme for internal reconstruction

lessons.title: AS 14: Types of Amalgamation and Purchase Consideration

scenes.text: Surat Textiles Ltd and Navsari Weaves Ltd agree to merge their operations into Surat Textiles.
Shareholders of Navsari want to know: how many shares and how much cash do we get?

steps.title: Merger: all five conditions
steps.body: An amalgamation is in the nature of merger only if: (1) all assets and liabilities of the transferor become those of the transferee; (2) holders of at least 90% of the face value of equity shares of the transferor (excluding those already held by the transferee) become equity shareholders of the transferee; (3) consideration to them is discharged wholly by equity shares, except cash for fractional shares; (4) the business of the transferor is intended to be carried on; (5) no adjustment is made to book values except to ensure uniform accounting policies. If any condition fails, it is an amalgamation in the nature of purchase.

steps.title: Purchase consideration
steps.body: AS 14 defines it as the aggregate of shares, other securities and cash or other assets paid by the transferee to the shareholders of the transferor. Payments to debenture-holders or creditors of the transferor are NOT part of purchase consideration; they are settlement of liabilities taken over.

steps.title: Worked example: net payment method
steps.body:
Navsari has 10,000 equity shares. For every 5 shares held, Surat issues 4 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹15, plus ₹5 cash per Navsari share.
Shares: 10,000 ÷ 5 × 4 = 8,000 shares × ₹15 = ₹1,20,000.
Cash: 10,000 × ₹5 = ₹50,000.
Purchase consideration = ₹1,70,000 (share capital ₹80,000, securities premium ₹40,000, cash ₹50,000).

steps.title: Worked example: net assets method
steps.body: Assets taken over at agreed values: land ₹2,00,000, plant ₹1,50,000, inventory ₹90,000, debtors ₹60,000 = ₹5,00,000. Liabilities taken over: creditors ₹1,00,000, 10% debentures ₹80,000 = ₹1,80,000. Purchase consideration = 5,00,000 − 1,80,000 = ₹3,20,000. Only assets and liabilities actually taken over, at their agreed (not book) values, are used.

steps.title: Intrinsic value method
steps.body: When the exchange ratio is based on the intrinsic value of shares, ratio = value of transferor share ÷ value of transferee share. If Navsari's share is worth ₹48 and Surat's ₹32, Surat issues 3 shares for every 2 Navsari shares.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Including amounts paid to debenture-holders or liquidation expenses borne by the transferee in purchase consideration, or using book values instead of agreed values under the net assets method.

activity.prompt: Transferor has 18,000 shares. Transferee issues 1 share of ₹10 at ₹12 for every 3 shares held, plus ₹1 cash per share held. Purchase consideration (₹)?

quiz.q: For a merger under AS 14, shareholders holding at least what share of face value must become shareholders of the transferee?
quiz.why: AS 14 requires holders of not less than 90% of the face value of the transferor's equity shares to become equity shareholders of the transferee.

quiz.q: Payment to debenture-holders of the transferor company is:
options: Settlement of a liability, not purchase consideration
quiz.why: Purchase consideration covers only payments to shareholders; debenture-holders are creditors whose liability is discharged.

quiz.q: If transferor share value is ₹60 and transferee share value is ₹40, the exchange ratio is:
quiz.why: Ratio = 60/40 = 1.5, so 3 transferee shares are issued for every 2 transferor shares.

quiz.q: Assets taken over ₹8 lakh and liabilities ₹2.5 lakh at agreed values. Purchase consideration by net assets method:
quiz.why: Net assets method gives assets minus liabilities taken over, 8 − 2.5 = ₹5.5 lakh.

lessons.title: Pooling of Interests vs Purchase Method: Entries

scenes.text: After the merger the accountant asks whether Navsari's general reserve survives in Surat's books.
Under pooling, yes. Under purchase, only statutory reserves are carried forward through an amalgamation adjustment account.

steps.title: Pooling of interests (merger)
steps.body: Assets, liabilities and reserves of the transferor are recorded at their existing carrying amounts (after aligning accounting policies). The difference between purchase consideration (share capital issued) and the share capital of the transferor is adjusted in reserves: excess consideration reduces reserves; shortfall is added to reserves.

steps.title: Purchase method
steps.body: Assets and liabilities are recorded at fair/agreed values. Reserves of the transferor (other than statutory reserves) are not carried forward. Excess of consideration over net assets = goodwill (amortised over not more than 5 years unless a longer period is justified); shortfall = capital reserve. Statutory reserves (e.g. export-profit reserve that must be kept for a period) are preserved: Dr Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve, Cr Statutory Reserve.

steps.title: Worked example: purchase method entries
steps.body:
Net assets at agreed values ₹3,20,000; purchase consideration ₹3,50,000 (equity 25,000 shares of ₹10 at ₹12 = ₹3,00,000 + cash ₹50,000).
1. Business Purchase A/c Dr 3,50,000 To Liquidator of Navsari 3,50,000.
2. Land, Plant, Inventory, Debtors Dr (agreed) 5,00,000; Goodwill Dr 30,000; To Creditors 1,00,000; To Debentures 80,000; To Business Purchase 3,50,000.
3. Liquidator Dr 3,50,000 To Equity Share Capital 2,50,000; To Securities Premium 50,000; To Bank 50,000.

steps.title: Worked example: pooling adjustment
steps.body: Transferor share capital ₹5,00,000; general reserve ₹2,00,000. Consideration: 60,000 shares of ₹10 = ₹6,00,000. Excess ₹1,00,000 is adjusted against reserves. General reserve carried forward = 2,00,000 − 1,00,000 = ₹1,00,000. No goodwill arises under pooling.

steps.title: Ind AS contrast
steps.body: Under Ind AS 103, pooling of interests is permitted only for common-control combinations (Appendix C); all other combinations use the acquisition method.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Recording goodwill under pooling, or forgetting that the transferor's statutory reserve must be carried forward under the purchase method.

activity.prompt: Order the entries in the transferee's books (purchase method).
items: Business Purchase A/c Dr, To Liquidator of transferor
Assets Dr (agreed values), Goodwill Dr, To Liabilities, To Business Purchase
Liquidator Dr, To Share Capital, To Securities Premium, To Bank
Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve Dr, To Statutory Reserve
Expenses of amalgamation paid by transferee Dr Goodwill/P&L, To Bank

quiz.q: Under pooling of interests, assets are recorded at:
quiz.why: Pooling simply combines existing carrying amounts, adjusted only for uniform accounting policies.

quiz.q: Under AS 14 purchase method, goodwill is normally amortised over not more than:
quiz.why: AS 14 requires amortisation over a period not exceeding five years unless a somewhat longer period can be justified.

quiz.q: If net assets exceed purchase consideration under the purchase method, the difference is:
quiz.why: A shortfall of consideration below net assets is credited to capital reserve.

quiz.q: Amalgamation Adjustment Reserve is debited to carry forward:
quiz.why: Statutory reserves must be preserved for legal reasons, so they are recreated with a matching debit to the adjustment reserve.

lessons.title: Ind AS 103: Acquisition Method, Goodwill and NCI

scenes.text: A Mumbai FMCG group buys 80% of a regional snacks company for ₹900 crore.
Goodwill depends on how the remaining 20% (non-controlling interest) is measured.

steps.title: Acquisition method steps
steps.body: 1. Identify the acquirer (the entity that obtains control, Ind AS 110). 2. Determine the acquisition date. 3. Recognise and measure identifiable assets acquired, liabilities assumed (at fair value) and any non-controlling interest. 4. Recognise goodwill or a bargain purchase gain.

steps.title: Goodwill formula
steps.body: Goodwill = Consideration transferred (at fair value, including contingent consideration) + NCI + fair value of previously held interest − fair value of identifiable net assets. NCI is measured either at fair value (full goodwill) or at NCI's proportionate share of identifiable net assets (partial goodwill), chosen per acquisition. Acquisition-related costs are expensed, not added to goodwill. Goodwill is not amortised; it is tested for impairment annually (Ind AS 36).

steps.title: Worked example: both NCI options
steps.body:
Consideration ₹900 crore for 80%. Fair value of identifiable net assets ₹1,000 crore. Fair value of NCI ₹250 crore.
Full goodwill: 900 + 250 − 1,000 = ₹150 crore.
Proportionate NCI: 20% × 1,000 = ₹200 crore; goodwill = 900 + 200 − 1,000 = ₹100 crore.
The ₹50 crore difference is goodwill attributable to the NCI.

steps.title: Worked example: bargain purchase
steps.body: Consideration ₹700 crore for 80%; net assets ₹1,000 crore; NCI proportionate ₹200 crore. 700 + 200 − 1,000 = −₹100 crore. After reassessing that all assets and liabilities are correctly identified and measured, Ind AS 103 (Indian carve-out) requires the gain to be recognised in OCI and accumulated in equity as capital reserve where there is clear evidence of a bargain purchase; otherwise it is recognised directly in capital reserve. It is not taken to profit or loss as under IFRS 3.

steps.title: Measurement period
steps.body: Provisional amounts may be adjusted retrospectively for up to one year from the acquisition date for new information about facts existing at that date.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Capitalising legal and due-diligence fees into goodwill, or amortising goodwill under Ind AS. Both are wrong: fees are expensed and goodwill is only impairment-tested.

activity.prompt: Consideration ₹540 crore for 75%; fair value of identifiable net assets ₹600 crore; NCI measured at proportionate share. Goodwill (₹ crore)?

quiz.q: Under Ind AS 103, acquisition-related costs are:
quiz.why: Ind AS 103 requires acquisition-related costs to be expensed in the periods they are incurred, except costs of issuing debt or equity.

quiz.q: Goodwill under Ind AS is:
options: Not amortised but tested annually for impairment
quiz.why: Ind AS 36 requires annual impairment testing of goodwill instead of amortisation.

quiz.q: Measuring NCI at fair value generally results in:
quiz.why: Fair value of NCI usually exceeds its proportionate share of net assets, so goodwill includes the NCI's portion.

quiz.q: Under Ind AS 103 in India, a bargain purchase gain with clear evidence is:
options: Deducted from goodwill of other subsidiaries
Recognised in OCI and accumulated as capital reserve
quiz.why: India's carve-out routes the gain to OCI and capital reserve rather than profit or loss.

scenes.text: A company has a debit balance in profit and loss of ₹4.5 lakh and a worthless goodwill of ₹1 lakh. It cannot pay dividends.
Shareholders agree to reduce each ₹10 share to ₹4 under a scheme approved by the Tribunal under Section 66.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: Internal reconstruction reorganises the capital structure without liquidating the company: reduction of share capital (Section 66, Companies Act 2013, with NCLT confirmation), alteration of share capital (Section 61: consolidation, sub-division), and compromise with creditors (Sections 230–232). The objective is to write off accumulated losses and fictitious/overvalued assets.

steps.title: Key entries
steps.body: Reduction: Equity Share Capital (old) Dr — To Equity Share Capital (new) — To Capital Reduction A/c. Use: Capital Reduction A/c Dr — To Profit and Loss (debit balance), To Goodwill, To Preliminary expenses, To assets written down. Balance left in Capital Reduction A/c is transferred to Capital Reserve.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
1,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 fully paid reduced to ₹4 each.
Reduction = 1,00,000 × 6 = ₹6,00,000.
Write-offs: P&L debit ₹4,50,000; goodwill ₹1,00,000. Total ₹5,50,000.
Balance ₹50,000 → Capital Reserve.
Revised share capital = ₹4,00,000.

steps.title: Worked example: with asset revaluation
steps.body: Capital reduction ₹3,00,000. Plant overvalued by ₹80,000 (write down), patents ₹40,000 worthless, P&L debit ₹1,50,000, land appreciated ₹20,000 (increase credited to Capital Reduction). Net debits = 80,000 + 40,000 + 1,50,000 − 20,000 = ₹2,50,000. Balance to capital reserve = ₹50,000.

steps.title: External vs internal
steps.body: External reconstruction winds up the old company and forms a new one to take over its business (accounted like amalgamation in the nature of purchase). Internal reconstruction keeps the same legal entity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Crediting the balance of Capital Reduction to general reserve or P&L — it is a capital profit and goes to capital reserve.

activity.prompt: 50,000 shares of ₹10 reduced to ₹3. Write off P&L debit ₹2,80,000 and patents ₹50,000. Transfer to capital reserve (₹)?

quiz.q: Reduction of share capital requires confirmation by the Tribunal under:
quiz.why: Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 governs reduction of share capital, which needs NCLT confirmation.

quiz.q: The balance in Capital Reduction Account after write-offs is transferred to:
quiz.why: It is a capital profit, so it is credited to capital reserve.

quiz.q: An increase in the value of land under a reconstruction scheme is:
quiz.why: Land Dr, To Capital Reduction records the appreciation as part of the scheme's resources.

quiz.q: In internal reconstruction the company:
options: Continues as the same legal entity
quiz.why: Internal reconstruction alters capital without liquidation, so the legal entity continues.

questions.q: Which is NOT a condition of amalgamation in the nature of merger?
options: All assets and liabilities taken over
Consideration only in equity shares except fractions
questions.why: A merger forbids adjustments to book values except for uniform policies.

Purchase consideration ₹4,00,000; net assets at agreed values ₹3,60,000 (purchase method). Goodwill:
questions.why: Excess of consideration over net assets, 4,00,000 − 3,60,000 = ₹40,000, is goodwill.

questions.q: Under pooling, transferor capital ₹4 lakh, consideration ₹3.5 lakh. The ₹0.5 lakh is:
questions.why: A shortfall of consideration below transferor's capital is added to reserves under pooling.

questions.q: Ind AS 103 requires pooling of interests for:
questions.why: Appendix C of Ind AS 103 applies pooling only to combinations under common control.

questions.q: Consideration ₹800; FV net assets ₹900; NCI 10% proportionate. Goodwill:
questions.why: 800 + 90 − 900 = −10, a bargain purchase gain of ₹10 after reassessment.

Due-diligence fees of ₹5 crore in an Ind AS 103 acquisition are:
questions.why: Acquisition-related costs are expensed.

questions.why: Provisional amounts may be finalised within one year from the acquisition date.

Capital reduction ₹2,00,000; P&L debit ₹1,20,000; goodwill ₹50,000; machinery appreciated ₹10,000. Capital reserve:
External reconstruction is accounted for like:
options: Amalgamation in the nature of purchase
questions.why: A new company takes over the old one's business; AS 14 treats it as purchase.
