courses.title: Unit 3 · Consolidated Financial Statements
courses.summary: Control under Ind AS 110, the consolidation procedure, goodwill and non-controlling interest, pre- and post-acquisition profits, elimination of intra-group items and unrealised profit, and the equity method for associates and joint ventures.
outcomes: Apply the three elements of control to decide whether an investee is a subsidiary
Compute goodwill/capital reserve, NCI and group reserves
Eliminate intra-group balances, transactions, dividends and unrealised profits
Account for associates and joint ventures by the equity method
Distinguish joint operations from joint ventures

scenes.text: An investor holds 45% of the votes; the remaining 55% is spread among thousands of retail holders who rarely vote.
Ind AS 110 looks at power, not just a 51% threshold — the investor may control the company.

steps.title: Definition of control
steps.body: An investor controls an investee when it has (1) power over the investee — existing rights giving the current ability to direct relevant activities; (2) exposure, or rights, to variable returns from its involvement; and (3) the ability to use its power to affect the amount of those returns. All three must be present. Potential voting rights that are substantive, contractual arrangements and de facto control (large holding versus dispersed others) are considered.

steps.title: Consolidation procedure
steps.body: 1. Use uniform accounting policies and the same reporting date (difference not more than three months, adjusted for significant transactions). 2. Combine like items of assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses and cash flows line by line. 3. Offset the parent's investment against its share of the subsidiary's equity, recognising goodwill or capital reserve. 4. Eliminate intra-group balances, transactions and unrealised profits in full. 5. Present NCI within equity, separately from the owners of the parent; attribute profit and OCI between owners of the parent and NCI.

steps.title: Legal requirement
steps.body: Section 129(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires a company with one or more subsidiaries, associates or joint ventures to prepare consolidated financial statements in addition to its standalone statements, and to attach a statement of salient features in Form AOC-1.

steps.title: Worked example: line-by-line
steps.body: H's inventory ₹6,00,000, S's inventory ₹2,50,000, of which ₹40,000 is unrealised intra-group profit. Consolidated inventory = 6,00,000 + 2,50,000 − 40,000 = ₹8,10,000. H's trade receivables include ₹30,000 due from S, which appears in S's payables: both are eliminated.

steps.title: Loss of control
steps.body: On losing control, derecognise the subsidiary's assets, liabilities and NCI, measure any retained interest at fair value, and recognise the gain or loss in profit or loss. Changes in ownership without loss of control are equity transactions — no gain or loss.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming more than 50% always means control (a contract may give power to another party) or that below 50% can never mean control.

activity.prompt: Order the consolidation procedure.
items: Align accounting policies and reporting dates
Add like items of assets, liabilities, income and expenses
Eliminate parent's investment against its share of subsidiary equity; recognise goodwill
Eliminate intra-group balances, transactions and unrealised profit
Compute and present NCI separately in equity

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three elements of control in Ind AS 110?
options: Ability to use power to affect returns
quiz.why: Ind AS 110 defines control through power, variable returns and their link; a 50% holding is only one way of getting power.

quiz.q: NCI is presented in the consolidated balance sheet:
options: Within equity, separately from parent's owners
quiz.why: Ind AS 110 requires NCI to be shown within equity, separate from the equity of the parent's owners.

quiz.q: The maximum gap between parent and subsidiary reporting dates allowed is:
quiz.why: Ind AS 110 permits the use of subsidiary statements with a date difference of not more than three months, adjusted for significant events.

quiz.q: Sale of a 10% stake in a subsidiary while keeping control is accounted as:
quiz.why: Changes in ownership that do not result in loss of control are transactions with owners recorded in equity.

scenes.text: H Ltd bought 80% of S Ltd on 1 April 2025. S's reserves on that day were ₹2 lakh; during FY 2025-26 S earned ₹3 lakh.
Only the ₹3 lakh earned after acquisition can be group profit; the ₹2 lakh is capital profit absorbed into goodwill.

steps.title: Analysis of profits
steps.body: Pre-acquisition profits (reserves and P&L balance on acquisition date) are capital profits: the parent's share goes to the cost-of-control (goodwill) computation. Post-acquisition profits are revenue profits: the parent's share is added to consolidated reserves. NCI gets its share of both. If acquisition happens mid-year, the year's profit is time-apportioned unless stated otherwise.

steps.title: Worked example: full computation
steps.body:
H paid ₹10,00,000 for 80% of S on 1 April 2025. S: share capital ₹8,00,000; reserves on 1 April 2025 ₹2,00,000; profit FY 2025-26 ₹3,00,000. NCI at proportionate share.
Step 1 – Net assets at acquisition = 8,00,000 + 2,00,000 = ₹10,00,000; H's share 80% = ₹8,00,000.
Step 2 – Goodwill = 10,00,000 − 8,00,000 = ₹2,00,000.
Step 3 – Post-acquisition profit ₹3,00,000: H's share ₹2,40,000 added to consolidated reserves; NCI share ₹60,000.
Step 4 – NCI at 31 March 2026 = 20% × (8,00,000 + 2,00,000 + 3,00,000) = ₹2,60,000.

steps.title: Worked example: mid-year acquisition
steps.body: Acquired 60% on 1 October 2025; S's profit for FY 2025-26 ₹4,80,000 earned evenly; reserves on 1 April 2025 ₹1,00,000. Pre-acquisition = 1,00,000 + 4,80,000 × 6/12 = ₹3,40,000. Post-acquisition = ₹2,40,000; H's share 60% = ₹1,44,000 to consolidated reserves.

steps.title: Fair value adjustments
steps.body: If S's land (book ₹5,00,000) is worth ₹6,00,000 at acquisition, net assets increase by ₹1,00,000 (less deferred tax under Ind AS 12), reducing goodwill. Upward revaluation of depreciable assets also requires extra depreciation post-acquisition, reducing post-acquisition profit.

steps.title: Bonus issue from pre-acquisition profits
steps.body: A bonus issue by S out of pre-acquisition reserves merely moves amounts within S's equity — it does not change goodwill.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Adding the parent's share of pre-acquisition reserves to consolidated reserves, or forgetting to give NCI its share of pre-acquisition reserves.

activity.prompt: H paid ₹7,50,000 for 60% of S. At acquisition S had share capital ₹10,00,000 and reserves ₹1,00,000 (book = fair value). Goodwill (₹)?

quiz.q: Parent's share of pre-acquisition profits of a subsidiary is:
quiz.why: Pre-acquisition profits are capital profits and form part of the net assets acquired, so they enter the goodwill computation.

quiz.q: S's post-acquisition profit ₹5 lakh; parent holds 70%. Amount added to consolidated reserves:
quiz.why: Only the parent's 70% share of post-acquisition profit, ₹3.5 lakh, belongs to group reserves.

quiz.q: An upward fair value adjustment of subsidiary land at acquisition:
quiz.why: Higher net assets acquired reduce the excess of consideration over net assets.

quiz.q: S's net assets at year-end ₹15 lakh; NCI 25% (proportionate). NCI:
quiz.why: Proportionate NCI equals 25% of ₹15 lakh, which is ₹3.75 lakh.

scenes.text: S sells goods to H at cost plus 25%. At year-end H still holds ₹50,000 of those goods.
The group cannot earn profit by trading with itself — the margin in unsold stock must be removed.

steps.title: What is eliminated
steps.body: Intra-group sales and purchases; inter-company loans, debentures and interest; trade receivables/payables between group companies (after adjusting cash/goods in transit); dividends paid by subsidiary to parent; unrealised profit in closing inventory and non-current assets transferred within the group. Bills receivable discounted with a bank are not eliminated, since they are owed to an outsider.

steps.title: Worked example: unrealised profit on cost
steps.body: Goods sold at cost + 25%; H holds ₹50,000 at invoice price. Profit in inventory = 50,000 × 25/125 = ₹10,000. Entry: Consolidated P&L (or reserves) Dr 10,000, To Inventory 10,000. Because this is an upstream sale (S → H) and NCI is 20%, ₹2,000 of the elimination is charged to NCI and ₹8,000 to the parent's owners. For a downstream sale (H → S) the whole elimination is borne by the parent's owners.

steps.title: Worked example: margin on sales
steps.body: Gross profit 20% on sales; closing inventory from group ₹60,000. Unrealised profit = 60,000 × 20% = ₹12,000. Note the difference from 'cost plus' wording: 20% on sales equals 25% on cost.

steps.title: Worked example: asset transfer
steps.body: On 1 April 2025, H sold a machine to S for ₹5,00,000; its carrying amount was ₹4,00,000. S depreciates at 10% straight-line. At 31 March 2026, unrealised profit remaining = 1,00,000 − 10% × 1,00,000 = ₹90,000. Reduce machinery and group reserves by ₹90,000.

steps.title: Dividends
steps.body: Dividend received by H from S's post-acquisition profits is income in H's standalone books but is eliminated on consolidation (it is a transfer within the group). The NCI portion of the dividend reduces NCI.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using 25% of invoice price when the margin is 25% on cost, or eliminating the whole intra-group sales figure from inventory instead of only the unrealised profit.

activity.prompt: S sells to H at cost plus 20%. H's closing inventory includes ₹72,000 of such goods. Unrealised profit to eliminate (₹)?

quiz.q: Goods sold at a profit of 25% on cost; inventory ₹1,00,000 at transfer price. Unrealised profit:
quiz.why: Profit is 25/125 of transfer price, so 1,00,000 × 25/125 = ₹20,000.

quiz.q: In an upstream sale with 30% NCI, the unrealised profit elimination is:
quiz.why: Upstream profit was recorded by the subsidiary, so its elimination is allocated between the parent's owners and NCI in their ownership ratio.

quiz.q: Bills drawn by H on S and discounted with a bank are:
quiz.why: Once discounted, the liability is owed to the bank, an outside party, so it remains in the consolidated statements.

quiz.q: Intra-group sales of ₹8 lakh during the year are:
options: Deducted from consolidated revenue and purchases
quiz.why: Both the sale and the matching purchase are internal and are eliminated from consolidated revenue and cost of sales.

lessons.title: Associates and Joint Arrangements: Equity Method

scenes.text: A company holds 30% of a logistics firm and nominates two of its eight directors.
It does not control the firm but has significant influence — so the investment is equity-accounted, not consolidated.

steps.title: Significant influence
steps.body: Ind AS 28: power to participate in financial and operating policy decisions without control. Presumed when the investor holds 20% or more of voting power, directly or indirectly (rebuttable). Evidence: board representation, participation in policy-making, material transactions, interchange of managerial personnel, provision of essential technical information.

steps.title: Equity method
steps.body: Initial recognition at cost. Afterwards: add the investor's share of profit (or deduct share of loss); add/deduct share of OCI; deduct dividends received (they return part of the investment). Any excess of cost over the share of net fair value is notional goodwill included in the carrying amount (not shown separately). Unrealised profits on transactions with the associate are eliminated to the extent of the investor's interest.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Investor buys 30% of A Ltd for ₹6,00,000 on 1 April 2025. A's profit for FY 2025-26 ₹4,00,000; dividend paid ₹1,00,000.
Share of profit = 30% × 4,00,000 = ₹1,20,000 (credit P&L).
Dividend received = 30% × 1,00,000 = ₹30,000 (credit investment).
Carrying amount at 31 March 2026 = 6,00,000 + 1,20,000 − 30,000 = ₹6,90,000.

steps.title: Joint arrangements (Ind AS 111)
steps.body: Joint control: contractually agreed sharing of control, decisions on relevant activities need unanimous consent. Joint operation: parties have rights to assets and obligations for liabilities — each records its share of assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses. Joint venture: parties have rights to the net assets (usually a separate vehicle) — equity method under Ind AS 28. Proportionate consolidation is not permitted for joint ventures.

steps.title: Losses beyond investment
steps.body: When the share of losses equals the carrying amount, the investor stops recognising further losses unless it has legal or constructive obligations; later profits are recognised only after the unrecognised losses are recovered.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Crediting dividends from an associate to P&L as income under the equity method — this double-counts profit already recognised.

activity.prompt: 25% of an associate bought for ₹8,00,000. Associate's profit ₹6,00,000 and dividend ₹2,00,000 in the year. Carrying amount at year-end (₹)?

quiz.q: Significant influence is presumed when an investor holds at least:
quiz.why: Ind AS 28 presumes significant influence at 20% or more of voting power unless clearly shown otherwise.

quiz.q: Under the equity method, dividends received are:
options: Deducted from the carrying amount of the investment
quiz.why: Dividends are a return of part of the investor's share of net assets, so they reduce the investment.

quiz.q: A joint venture is accounted for by:
quiz.why: Ind AS 111 requires joint ventures to be accounted for using the equity method under Ind AS 28.

quiz.q: In a joint operation, each party recognises:
options: Its share of assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses
quiz.why: Joint operators have direct rights and obligations, so they record their own share of each item.

questions.q: Consolidated financial statements are required by:
questions.why: Section 129(3) of the Companies Act requires consolidation when a company has subsidiaries, associates or JVs.

questions.q: H paid ₹9 lakh for 75% of S whose net assets were ₹10 lakh. Goodwill (proportionate NCI):
Using the same data, NCI at acquisition:
questions.why: NCI = 25% × ₹10 lakh = ₹2.5 lakh.

questions.q: Acquisition on 1 July; S's annual profit ₹12 lakh earned evenly; year ends 31 March. Post-acquisition profit:
questions.why: Nine months fall after 1 July, so 12 × 9/12 = ₹9 lakh.

questions.q: Profit is 20% on sales; group inventory ₹45,000. Unrealised profit:
Downstream sale unrealised profit ₹10,000; NCI 20%. Charge to NCI:
questions.why: In a downstream sale the profit sits in the parent's books, so the whole elimination is borne by the parent's owners.

questions.q: Machine sold within group at a profit of ₹2 lakh; buyer depreciates 20% SLM. Unrealised profit after one year:
questions.why: 20% of the profit is realised through depreciation, leaving 2 × 0.8 = ₹1.6 lakh.

questions.q: Which is NOT eliminated on consolidation?
questions.why: Discounted bills are a liability to the bank, an outsider.

questions.q: Investor's 40% of associate profit ₹5 lakh; dividend received ₹0.8 lakh; cost ₹10 lakh. Carrying amount:
Proportionate consolidation for joint ventures under Ind AS is:
questions.why: Ind AS 111 requires the equity method for joint ventures.

questions.q: Loss of control of a subsidiary results in:
options: Remeasuring retained interest at fair value and a gain/loss in P&L
questions.why: Ind AS 110 derecognises the subsidiary and remeasures any retained stake at fair value through P&L.

questions.q: S's land book value ₹5 lakh, fair value ₹7 lakh at acquisition (ignore tax). Effect on goodwill:
options: Decrease by parent's share of ₹2 lakh (proportionate NCI)
questions.why: Net assets rise by ₹2 lakh, so goodwill falls by the parent's share of that increase when NCI is proportionate.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Valuation of Goodwill & Shares, Financial Instruments and Leases
courses.summary: Valuing goodwill (average profit, super profit, capitalisation and annuity methods) and shares (net assets, yield and fair value), classifying and measuring financial instruments under Ind AS 32/109 with the effective interest method, and lessee accounting under Ind AS 116.
outcomes: Value goodwill by average profit, super profit, capitalisation and annuity methods
Value equity shares by intrinsic, yield and fair value methods
Classify financial assets as amortised cost, FVOCI or FVTPL and apply the effective interest method
Measure a lease liability and right-of-use asset and prepare the first-year entries

scenes.text: A Chennai café chain earns ₹2.4 lakh a year more than a normal café with the same capital would.
A buyer will pay for that extra earning power — that is goodwill.

steps.title: Meaning and factors
steps.body: Goodwill is the present value of a firm's expected future earnings in excess of the normal return on capital employed. Factors: location, management quality, brand, customer base, monopoly or licences, efficient processes. Purchased goodwill is recognised in the accounts; self-generated goodwill is not (Ind AS 38).

steps.title: Methods and formulas
steps.body:
Average profit method: Goodwill = Average maintainable profit × number of years' purchase.
Super profit = Average profit − Normal profit, where Normal profit = Capital employed × Normal rate of return (NRR).
Super profit method: Goodwill = Super profit × years' purchase.
Capitalisation of super profit: Goodwill = Super profit × 100 / NRR.
Capitalisation of average profit: Goodwill = (Average profit × 100 / NRR) − Capital employed.
Annuity method: Goodwill = Super profit × PV annuity factor at NRR for the given years.

steps.title: Worked example: all methods
steps.body:
Profits: ₹2,00,000; ₹2,40,000; ₹2,80,000 → average ₹2,40,000. Capital employed ₹15,00,000; NRR 12%.
Normal profit = 15,00,000 × 12% = ₹1,80,000; super profit = ₹60,000.
(a) Super profit, 3 years' purchase: 60,000 × 3 = ₹1,80,000.
(b) Capitalisation of super profit: 60,000 × 100/12 = ₹5,00,000.
(c) Capitalisation of average profit: 2,40,000 × 100/12 = 20,00,000 − 15,00,000 = ₹5,00,000 (same as b, as it should be).
(d) Annuity, 3 years at 12% (PVAF 2.4018): 60,000 × 2.4018 = ₹1,44,108.

steps.title: Adjusting profits
steps.body: Use maintainable profits: remove abnormal gains/losses (profit on sale of a fixed asset, loss by fire), adjust for under/over-charged depreciation or managerial remuneration, deduct tax, and give weights if a trend exists (weighted average — higher weights to recent years). Capital employed = assets (excluding goodwill and non-trade investments) at current values − outside liabilities; average capital employed = closing − ½ of current year's profit after tax.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Including goodwill or fictitious assets in capital employed, or using pre-tax profit when NRR is a post-tax rate.

activity.prompt: Average profit ₹1,50,000; capital employed ₹10,00,000; NRR 10%. Goodwill at 4 years' purchase of super profit (₹)?

quiz.q: Super profit equals:
quiz.why: Super profit is the excess of average maintainable profit over the normal return on capital employed.

quiz.q: Super profit ₹40,000 and NRR 8%. Goodwill by capitalising super profit:
Which asset is excluded from capital employed?
quiz.why: Non-trade investments do not earn trading profit, so they and their income are excluded.

quiz.q: Self-generated goodwill under Ind AS 38 is:
quiz.why: Internally generated goodwill cannot be measured reliably and is not recognised as an asset.

scenes.text: A family wants to sell its 10% stake in an unlisted Kolkata engineering company. There is no stock-market price.
The valuer computes intrinsic value from net assets and yield value from expected dividends.

steps.title: Net assets (intrinsic) method
steps.body: Value per equity share = (Total assets at realisable/fair value, including goodwill − outside liabilities − preference share capital and arrears of preference dividend if payable) ÷ number of equity shares. Suited to controlling stakes and liquidation.

steps.title: Worked example: intrinsic value
steps.body:
Assets at fair value (including goodwill) ₹25,00,000; liabilities ₹7,00,000; 10% preference capital ₹3,00,000; 50,000 equity shares of ₹10.
Net assets for equity = 25,00,000 − 7,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹15,00,000.
Value per share = 15,00,000 ÷ 50,000 = ₹30.

steps.title: Yield (market value) method
steps.body: Value per share = (Expected rate of dividend or earnings ÷ Normal rate of return) × paid-up value per share. Expected dividend rate = profit available for equity dividend (after tax, transfers to reserves and preference dividend) ÷ paid-up equity capital × 100. Suited to minority stakes, who receive only dividends.

steps.title: Worked example: yield and fair value
steps.body:
Expected equity dividend rate 18%; normal rate for similar shares 12%; paid-up value ₹10. Yield value = 18/12 × 10 = ₹15.
Fair value = (Intrinsic + Yield)/2 = (30 + 15)/2 = ₹22.50.

steps.title: Partly paid shares
steps.body: With fully and partly paid shares, add notional calls to net assets, divide by total number of shares to get value of a fully paid share, then deduct the unpaid amount for partly paid shares.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting to deduct preference capital, or using face value instead of paid-up value in the yield formula.

activity.prompt: Assets at fair value ₹18,00,000; liabilities ₹4,00,000; preference capital ₹2,00,000; 60,000 equity shares. Intrinsic value per share (₹)?

quiz.q: Expected dividend 15%, NRR 10%, paid-up value ₹100. Yield value:
Intrinsic value ₹40 and yield value ₹30. Fair value:
quiz.why: Fair value is the simple average (40 + 30)/2 = ₹35.

quiz.q: The yield method suits valuation of:
quiz.why: Minority holders cannot influence asset use and mainly receive dividends, so the yield basis is appropriate.

quiz.q: In the net assets method, preference capital is:
quiz.why: Preference shareholders have a prior claim on assets, so their capital is deducted before dividing among equity shares.

scenes.text: A company issues redeemable preference shares with a fixed 8% dividend.
Ind AS 32 looks at substance: a contractual obligation to pay cash makes it a financial liability, not equity.

steps.title: Liability vs equity (Ind AS 32)
steps.body: A financial liability is a contractual obligation to deliver cash or another financial asset. Equity is a residual interest with no such obligation. Mandatorily redeemable preference shares with fixed dividends are liabilities; their dividend is interest expense. A compound instrument (e.g. convertible debentures) is split: liability component = PV of cash flows at the market rate for similar non-convertible debt; equity component = proceeds − liability component.

steps.title: Classification of financial assets (Ind AS 109)
steps.body: Based on (1) the business model and (2) contractual cash-flow characteristics (SPPI — solely payments of principal and interest). Amortised cost: held to collect, SPPI. FVOCI (debt): held to collect and sell, SPPI. FVTPL: everything else (trading, derivatives). Equity investments not held for trading may be irrevocably designated at FVOCI; then gains are never recycled to P&L.

steps.title: Worked example: effective interest method
steps.body:
A loan of ₹1,00,000 is given; the borrower will repay ₹1,21,000 after 2 years, no coupon. EIR solves 1,00,000 × (1 + r)² = 1,21,000 → r = 10%.
Year 1 interest = 10% × 1,00,000 = ₹10,000; carrying amount ₹1,10,000.
Year 2 interest = 10% × 1,10,000 = ₹11,000; carrying amount ₹1,21,000 = repayment.

steps.title: Worked example: compound instrument
steps.body: Convertible debentures issued for ₹10,00,000; PV of interest and principal at the 12% market rate for straight debt = ₹9,27,880 (given). Liability component ₹9,27,880; equity component = 10,00,000 − 9,27,880 = ₹72,120, credited to other equity.

steps.title: Impairment
steps.body: Ind AS 109 uses an expected credit loss (ECL) model: 12-month ECL at initial recognition, lifetime ECL when credit risk increases significantly; trade receivables may use the simplified approach (lifetime ECL, often via a provision matrix).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating redeemable preference share dividend as an appropriation of profit under Ind AS — it is a finance cost.

activity.prompt: Lender pays ₹5,00,000 and receives ₹6,05,000 after 2 years (EIR 10%). Interest income in year 1 (₹)?

quiz.q: A debt instrument held to collect contractual cash flows that are SPPI is measured at:
quiz.why: Ind AS 109 measures held-to-collect SPPI assets at amortised cost.

quiz.q: Mandatorily redeemable preference shares are classified as:
quiz.why: The issuer has a contractual obligation to pay cash, which meets the definition of a financial liability.

quiz.q: Gains on equity investments designated at FVOCI are:
quiz.why: The FVOCI election for equity is irrevocable and amounts in OCI are not reclassified to profit or loss.

quiz.q: Convertible debentures proceeds ₹50 lakh; liability component ₹46 lakh. Equity component:
quiz.why: The equity component is the residual, 50 − 46 = ₹4 lakh.

scenes.text: A retailer rents a warehouse for 3 years at ₹1 lakh a year, paid at year-end.
Under Ind AS 116 the rent is no longer just an expense: the lessee records a right-of-use asset and a lease liability.

steps.title: Single lessee model
steps.body: At commencement the lessee recognises a lease liability = PV of unpaid lease payments, discounted at the interest rate implicit in the lease or, if not determinable, the incremental borrowing rate; and a right-of-use (ROU) asset = lease liability + initial direct costs + payments made at or before commencement − incentives + restoration costs. Exemptions: short-term leases (12 months or less) and leases of low-value assets may be expensed.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Payments ₹1,00,000 at the end of each year for 3 years; rate 10%; PVAF(10%, 3) = 2.48685.
Lease liability = ROU asset = ₹2,48,685.
Year 1: interest = 24,869; payment 1,00,000; closing liability = 2,48,685 + 24,869 − 1,00,000 = ₹1,73,554.
Depreciation of ROU (SLM, 3 years) = 2,48,685 ÷ 3 = ₹82,895.
Total year-1 expense = 24,869 + 82,895 = ₹1,07,764 (higher than the ₹1,00,000 rent; the expense is front-loaded).

steps.title: Entries
steps.body: Commencement: ROU Asset Dr 2,48,685, To Lease Liability 2,48,685. Year-end: Interest on Lease Liability Dr 24,869, To Lease Liability 24,869; Lease Liability Dr 1,00,000, To Bank 1,00,000; Depreciation Dr 82,895, To ROU Asset 82,895.

steps.title: Lessor side in brief
steps.body: Lessors still classify leases as finance (substantially all risks and rewards transferred — recognise a lease receivable) or operating (keep the asset, recognise rent income on a straight-line basis).

steps.title: Cash-flow statement
steps.body: Principal repayments of lease liabilities are financing cash flows; interest follows the entity's policy (financing or operating); short-term lease payments are operating.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the annuity-due factor when payments are in arrears, or depreciating the ROU asset over the useful life of the building instead of the lease term (unless ownership transfers).

activity.prompt: Using the worked example (opening liability in year 2 = ₹1,73,554, rate 10%), what is interest for year 2 to the nearest rupee?

quiz.q: A lessee may elect not to recognise an ROU asset for leases of:
quiz.why: Ind AS 116 allows a short-term lease exemption for leases with a term of 12 months or less.

quiz.q: The lease liability is initially measured at:
quiz.why: The liability equals the present value of lease payments not yet paid at commencement.

quiz.q: Under Ind AS 116, total lessee expense in early years is usually:
quiz.why: Interest is highest when the liability is largest, so interest plus depreciation is front-loaded.

quiz.q: Principal repayment of a lease liability is classified in cash flows as:
quiz.why: Repaying the principal of a liability is a financing activity under Ind AS 7.

questions.q: Profits ₹90,000, ₹1,10,000, ₹1,30,000. Goodwill at 2 years' purchase of average profit:
Capital employed ₹8,00,000; NRR 10%; average profit ₹1,00,000. Super profit:
questions.why: Normal profit ₹80,000, so super profit = ₹20,000.

questions.q: Super profit ₹30,000; NRR 15%. Goodwill by capitalisation of super profit:
Super profit ₹50,000; PVAF 10%, 4 years = 3.1699. Goodwill by annuity method:
Weights 1, 2, 3 on profits ₹60,000, ₹90,000, ₹1,20,000. Weighted average profit:
Net assets for equity ₹9,00,000; 30,000 shares. Intrinsic value:
Expected dividend 12%, NRR 16%, paid-up ₹10. Yield value:
Derivatives not designated as hedges are measured at:
questions.why: Derivatives fail SPPI and are held at fair value through profit or loss.

questions.q: Loan ₹2,00,000, EIR 12%; no cash in year 1. Carrying amount at end of year 1:
The ECL simplified approach for trade receivables recognises:
questions.why: Ind AS 109 permits lifetime ECL from initial recognition for trade receivables.

questions.q: Lease liability ₹5,00,000 at 8%; first annual payment in arrears ₹1,50,000. Closing liability year 1:
ROU asset ₹6,00,000; lease term 5 years; useful life 8 years; no ownership transfer. Annual depreciation:
questions.why: Depreciate over the shorter of lease term and useful life: 6,00,000 ÷ 5 = ₹1,20,000.

outcomes: Recall all key Ind AS rules and valuation formulas from the course
Prepare a consolidated balance sheet working from raw data

Answer long exam questions in a structured, marks-oriented way

scenes.text: Ananya has 10 hours before her M.Com semester paper and five units to revise.
She uses one sheet: every rule and formula that earns marks.

steps.title: Ind AS essentials
steps.body: Ind AS 1: complete set = BS, P&L with OCI, SOCE, cash flows, notes, comparatives (+ third BS when restated). Ind AS 8: policy change & errors → retrospective; estimate change → prospective. Ind AS 10: adjusting vs non-adjusting; dividends declared after year-end not a liability. Ind AS 115: 5 steps; allocate on relative standalone selling prices; constraint on variable consideration.

steps.title: Combinations and reconstruction
steps.body: Purchase consideration = payments to shareholders only. Net assets method = assets taken over − liabilities taken over (agreed values). AS 14 merger: 5 conditions; pooling at book values. Purchase: goodwill amortised ≤ 5 years; capital reserve if negative. Ind AS 103: Goodwill = Consideration + NCI + previously held interest − FV net assets; costs expensed; bargain gain → OCI/capital reserve. Capital reduction balance → capital reserve.

steps.title: Consolidation
steps.body: Control = power + variable returns + link. Goodwill = cost − parent's share of net assets at acquisition. NCI = NCI% × net assets at reporting date (proportionate). Unrealised profit: cost-plus x% → x/(100 + x) of transfer price; margin on sales y% → y% of transfer price. Upstream elimination shared with NCI. Associate carrying amount = cost + share of profit − dividends received.

steps.title: Valuation, instruments, leases
steps.body: Super profit = average profit − CE × NRR. Capitalisation: SP × 100/NRR. Annuity: SP × PVAF. Intrinsic = (assets − liabilities − preference capital)/equity shares. Yield = (expected rate/NRR) × paid-up value. Fair value = average. Ind AS 109: amortised cost / FVOCI / FVTPL; EIR interest = opening carrying × EIR. Ind AS 116: liability = PV of payments; interest = opening × rate; ROU depreciated over shorter of lease term and life.

steps.title: Answer-writing tip
steps.body: In numericals, always show a 'Working Notes' block: (1) analysis of profits, (2) goodwill, (3) NCI, (4) consolidated reserves. Examiners award step marks even if the final figure is wrong.

steps.title: Top five exam errors
steps.body: 1. Including debenture-holders in purchase consideration. 2. Pre-acquisition profit added to group reserves. 3. 25% on cost applied as 25% of transfer price. 4. Crediting associate dividends to P&L. 5. Amortising Ind AS goodwill.

activity.prompt: Complete the key rules.
activity.text: A change in accounting estimate is applied ___. Under Ind AS 103 acquisition costs are ___. Profit of 25% on cost equals ___% of transfer price.

quiz.q: Which is applied retrospectively?
quiz.why: Ind AS 8 requires prior-period errors to be corrected retrospectively; estimate changes are prospective.

quiz.q: Profit of 50% on cost equals what share of transfer price?
quiz.why: 50/150 = one-third of the transfer price.

quiz.q: Capital employed for goodwill valuation excludes:
quiz.why: Goodwill being valued cannot be part of the capital base that earns normal profit.

scenes.text: Your practical file asks for a full consolidated balance sheet of H Ltd and its subsidiary S Ltd.
Work the four standard notes, then fill the figures.

steps.title: Data
steps.body: On 1 April 2025 H acquired 80% of S for ₹6,00,000. S at 1 April 2025: share capital ₹5,00,000; reserves ₹1,00,000. S at 31 March 2026: share capital ₹5,00,000; reserves ₹1,00,000; P&L (current year) ₹1,50,000. H's own reserves at 31 March 2026: ₹4,00,000. S sold goods to H at cost + 25%; H's closing inventory includes ₹25,000 of these. H owes S ₹20,000. NCI at proportionate share.

steps.title: Note 1: analysis of S's profits
steps.body: Pre-acquisition (capital): reserves ₹1,00,000. Post-acquisition (revenue): ₹1,50,000 less unrealised profit 25,000 × 25/125 = ₹5,000 → ₹1,45,000 (upstream, so shared). H 80% = ₹1,16,000; NCI 20% = ₹29,000.

steps.title: Notes 3 and 4: NCI and reserves
steps.body:
NCI = 20% × (5,00,000 + 1,00,000) + 29,000 = 1,20,000 + 29,000 = ₹1,49,000.
Consolidated reserves = H's 4,00,000 + 1,16,000 = ₹5,16,000.
Inventory is reduced by ₹5,000; mutual owing of ₹20,000 removed from both receivables and payables.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body: Q: Why is the ₹5,000 shared with NCI? A: The sale was upstream, so S recorded the profit. Q: Why is ₹1,00,000 not in consolidated reserves? A: It is pre-acquisition and absorbed into goodwill. Q: Where does NCI appear? A: Within equity, separately.

activity.prompt: In the lab data, if H's closing inventory from S had been ₹50,000 instead of ₹25,000, what would NCI be (₹)?

quiz.q: In the lab, goodwill is:
quiz.why: Cost ₹6,00,000 minus 80% of ₹6,00,000 net assets at acquisition gives ₹1,20,000.

quiz.q: In the lab, consolidated reserves are:
quiz.why: H's ₹4,00,000 plus its 80% share of adjusted post-acquisition profit ₹1,16,000 equals ₹5,16,000.

quiz.q: The ₹20,000 owed by H to S is:
quiz.why: Intra-group balances cancel because the group cannot owe itself money.

lessons.title: Lab: Amalgamation from Start to Finish

scenes.text: A Ltd takes over B Ltd. You must compute purchase consideration and pass entries in A's books under the purchase method.
Follow the order an examiner expects.

steps.title: Data
steps.body: B Ltd: 40,000 equity shares of ₹10; land ₹3,00,000 (agreed ₹4,00,000); plant ₹2,00,000 (agreed ₹1,80,000); inventory ₹1,20,000 (agreed ₹1,00,000); debtors ₹80,000; creditors ₹1,00,000; general reserve ₹1,00,000. Consideration: 3 shares of A (₹10 each, issued at ₹15) for every 4 shares of B, plus ₹2 cash per B share.

steps.title: Step 2: net assets and goodwill
steps.body: Assets at agreed values = 4,00,000 + 1,80,000 + 1,00,000 + 80,000 = ₹7,60,000. Less creditors ₹1,00,000 = ₹6,60,000. Purchase consideration ₹5,30,000 < ₹6,60,000 → capital reserve ₹1,30,000. B's general reserve is not carried forward.

steps.title: Step 3: entries
steps.body: Business Purchase Dr 5,30,000 To Liquidator of B 5,30,000. Land 4,00,000, Plant 1,80,000, Inventory 1,00,000, Debtors 80,000 Dr; To Creditors 1,00,000; To Business Purchase 5,30,000; To Capital Reserve 1,30,000. Liquidator Dr 5,30,000; To Equity Share Capital 3,00,000; To Securities Premium 1,50,000; To Bank 80,000.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body: Q: Why is the general reserve not recorded? A: Under the purchase method only statutory reserves are carried forward. Q: What changes under pooling? A: Book values and reserves would be recorded; difference adjusted in reserves; no capital reserve.

items: Compute purchase consideration

Pass journal entries in the transferee's books

quiz.why: Shares worth ₹4,50,000 plus cash ₹80,000 make ₹5,30,000.

A structured table and one example score better than a page of prose.

steps.title: Q1 (10 marks): Pooling vs purchase
steps.body: Model answer points: basis (merger vs purchase); values (book vs fair/agreed); reserves (all carried vs only statutory); difference (adjusted in reserves vs goodwill/capital reserve); goodwill (never vs possible, amortised ≤ 5 years); Ind AS position (pooling only for common control). Close with a two-line numerical illustration.

steps.title: Q2 (10 marks): Explain control under Ind AS 110 with examples
steps.body: Define control and its three elements; explain power (voting rights, potential voting rights, contractual rights, de facto control); returns (dividends, synergies, fees); link (agent vs principal). Example: 45% holder with dispersed shareholders controls; 60% holder whose rights are given to a manager under contract may not.

Q4 (6 marks): Short notes

steps.title: Time plan
steps.body: For a 3-hour, 80-mark paper: about 2 minutes per mark, leaving 15 minutes to check workings.

questions.why: The unused balance 5 − 4.2 = ₹0.8 lakh goes to capital reserve.

questions.why: NCI 10% × ₹2 lakh = ₹0.2 lakh.

questions.why: Profit is 1/4 of transfer price (1/3 ÷ 4/3), so 40,000 ÷ 4 = ₹10,000.

Fall in market value of investments after year-end

uni-mcom-corporate-financial-management.title: M.Com · Corporate Financial Management
uni-mcom-corporate-financial-management.description: Capital budgeting, cost of capital, capital structure and leverage, dividend decisions and working capital management with fully solved numericals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian M.Com programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Capital Budgeting
courses.summary: Estimating incremental after-tax cash flows and evaluating projects by payback, ARR, NPV, profitability index and IRR; resolving NPV–IRR conflicts; and handling risk and capital rationing.
outcomes: Estimate relevant incremental cash flows after tax
Compute payback, discounted payback and ARR
Compute NPV, PI and IRR and interpret them
Explain and resolve NPV–IRR ranking conflicts
Apply risk-adjusted discount rate, certainty equivalent and capital rationing

lessons.title: Cash Flow Estimation, Payback and ARR

scenes.text: A Nagpur beverage firm can buy a ₹10 lakh bottling line. The board wants to know: when do we get our money back?
First, convert accounting profit into after-tax cash flows — depreciation is not a cash outflow.

steps.title: Relevant cash flows
steps.body: Use incremental, after-tax cash flows. Include: initial outlay (cost + installation + increase in working capital), operating cash flows, terminal cash flows (salvage after tax + release of working capital). Ignore sunk costs; include opportunity costs; ignore financing costs (interest is reflected in the discount rate).

steps.title: CFAT formula
steps.body: CFAT = (Revenue − Cash costs − Depreciation)(1 − t) + Depreciation = (Revenue − Cash costs)(1 − t) + t × Depreciation. The term t × Depreciation is the depreciation tax shield.

steps.title: Worked example: payback
steps.body:
Cost ₹10,00,000; CFAT ₹3,00,000, ₹4,00,000, ₹5,00,000, ₹2,00,000.
Cumulative: 3,00,000 (yr 1), 7,00,000 (yr 2). Remaining ₹3,00,000 of ₹5,00,000 in year 3 → 0.6 year. Payback = 2.6 years. With equal annual CFAT, payback = cost ÷ annual CFAT.

steps.title: Accounting rate of return
steps.body: ARR = Average annual profit after tax ÷ Average investment × 100, where average investment = (initial cost − salvage)/2 + salvage (+ working capital). Example: average PAT ₹60,000, cost ₹4,00,000, no salvage → average investment ₹2,00,000 → ARR 30%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Deducting interest from cash flows (double-counts the cost of finance) or including a sunk feasibility study cost. Payback also ignores time value and cash flows after the payback period — use it as a liquidity screen, not the decision rule.

activity.prompt: Revenue ₹8,00,000; cash costs ₹3,00,000; depreciation ₹2,00,000; tax 30%. CFAT (₹)?

quiz.q: Which is NOT a relevant cash flow?
options: Sunk cost of a past survey
quiz.why: Sunk costs have already been incurred and do not change with the decision, so they are excluded.

quiz.q: Cost ₹6 lakh; equal CFAT ₹1.5 lakh a year. Payback:
quiz.why: With equal flows, payback = 6 ÷ 1.5 = 4 years.

quiz.q: Depreciation tax shield with depreciation ₹2 lakh and tax 25%:
quiz.why: Tax shield = tax rate × depreciation = 0.25 × 2 = ₹0.5 lakh.

quiz.q: A major limitation of payback is that it:
options: Ignores cash flows after the payback period
quiz.why: Payback stops counting at recovery, so a project with large later inflows may be wrongly rejected.

scenes.text: ₹5 lakh received in year 3 is worth less than ₹5 lakh today.
Discount every flow at the cost of capital and add them: if the total beats the cost, the project creates value.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: NPV = Σ CFₜ/(1 + k)ᵗ − Initial outlay. Accept if NPV > 0. PI (benefit–cost ratio) = PV of inflows ÷ PV of outflows. Accept if PI > 1. NPV is consistent with shareholder-wealth maximisation and is additive across projects.

steps.title: Worked example: annuity
steps.body:
Cost ₹50,000; CFAT ₹20,000 a year for 3 years; k = 10%; PVAF(10%, 3) = 2.4869.
PV = 20,000 × 2.4869 = ₹49,738. NPV = −₹262 → reject (marginally).

steps.title: Discounted payback
steps.body: Cumulate discounted CFAT until it equals the outlay. In the first example: 2,72,730; 6,03,290; 9,78,940; then the remaining ₹21,060 of ₹1,36,600 → 0.15 year. Discounted payback ≈ 3.15 years.

steps.title: When PI helps
steps.body: Under capital rationing with divisible projects, rank by PI to maximise total NPV within the budget.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the release of working capital and after-tax salvage in the final year, or discounting year-0 outlay.

activity.prompt: Cost ₹2,00,000; CFAT ₹80,000 a year for 4 years; k = 12%; PVAF(12%, 4) = 3.0373. NPV (₹)?

quiz.q: A project is acceptable when:
quiz.why: A positive NPV means discounted inflows exceed the outlay, creating wealth for shareholders.

quiz.q: PV of inflows ₹12 lakh; outlay ₹10 lakh. PI:
NPV is additive, which means:
quiz.why: Value additivity lets combined projects be evaluated by summing their NPVs, which IRR does not allow.

quiz.q: Discounted payback is always:
options: Longer than or equal to simple payback
quiz.why: Discounting reduces each inflow, so recovery takes at least as long.

scenes.text: The CFO asks: at what discount rate would this project's NPV be exactly zero?
That rate is the internal rate of return; compare it with the cost of capital.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: IRR is the rate r at which Σ CFₜ/(1 + r)ᵗ = Initial outlay, i.e. NPV = 0. Accept if IRR > cost of capital. Found by trial and error with interpolation: IRR = L + (NPV at L) ÷ (NPV at L − NPV at H) × (H − L).

steps.title: Why NPV and IRR conflict
steps.body: For mutually exclusive projects, rankings may differ due to (1) size disparity, (2) timing disparity of cash flows, (3) unequal lives. The reason is the reinvestment assumption: NPV assumes reinvestment at the cost of capital (realistic); IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself. Resolve by NPV, or by modified IRR (MIRR), or incremental IRR on the difference between the projects. Non-conventional flows (sign changes more than once) may give multiple IRRs.

steps.title: Fisher's intersection
steps.body: The discount rate at which NPV profiles of two projects cross; below it the projects rank differently by NPV than by IRR.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Interpolating between rates that are far apart (e.g. 10% and 30%) — the NPV curve is convex, so keep the rates close for accuracy.

activity.prompt: NPV at 12% = ₹24,000; NPV at 14% = −₹6,000. Interpolated IRR (%)?

quiz.q: IRR is the rate at which:
quiz.why: By definition, IRR equates the PV of inflows with the outlay, making NPV zero.

quiz.q: For mutually exclusive projects with conflicting ranks, prefer:
quiz.why: NPV directly measures wealth added and assumes a realistic reinvestment rate.

quiz.q: IRR implicitly assumes reinvestment at:
quiz.why: The IRR calculation implies intermediate flows earn the IRR, which is often unrealistic.

quiz.q: Multiple IRRs can arise when:
options: The cost of capital is high
Cash flows change sign more than once
quiz.why: By Descartes' rule of signs, each sign change can create another root of the NPV equation.

scenes.text: A fertiliser plant's sales depend on the monsoon. Cash flows are uncertain.
Finance managers adjust either the discount rate or the cash flows for risk.

steps.title: Risk-adjusted discount rate (RADR)
steps.body: Discount at k = risk-free rate + risk premium. Riskier projects get a higher rate. Simple, but it assumes risk grows with time in a compounding way.

steps.title: Worked example: certainty equivalent
steps.body:
Expected CFAT year 1 ₹1,00,000; certainty-equivalent coefficient 0.8; risk-free rate 6%.
Certain cash flow = 0.8 × 1,00,000 = ₹80,000. PV = 80,000/1.06 = ₹75,472. Sum for all years and subtract the outlay to get the CE-NPV, discounted at the risk-free rate.

steps.title: Sensitivity, scenario, simulation, decision tree
steps.body: Sensitivity analysis changes one variable at a time (price, volume, cost) to find break-even values. Scenario analysis changes several variables together (pessimistic/most likely/optimistic). Monte Carlo simulation draws thousands of combinations to get an NPV distribution. Decision trees map sequential decisions and probabilities: expected NPV = Σ probability × NPV.

steps.title: Worked example: expected NPV
steps.body: NPV ₹8 lakh with probability 0.3, ₹3 lakh with 0.5, −₹4 lakh with 0.2. Expected NPV = 2.4 + 1.5 − 0.8 = ₹3.1 lakh.

steps.title: Capital rationing
steps.body: When funds are limited: for divisible projects, rank by PI and accept in order, taking a fraction of the last; for indivisible projects, test feasible combinations within the budget and choose the one with the highest total NPV.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Discounting certainty-equivalent cash flows at the risk-adjusted rate — that double-counts risk; use the risk-free rate.

activity.prompt: NPVs ₹10 lakh (p = 0.25), ₹4 lakh (p = 0.5), −₹2 lakh (p = 0.25). Expected NPV (₹ lakh)?

quiz.q: Certainty-equivalent cash flows are discounted at:
quiz.why: Risk has already been removed from the cash flows, so only time value remains.

quiz.q: Sensitivity analysis changes:
quiz.why: It isolates the effect of each variable on NPV by changing them one at a time.

quiz.q: Under capital rationing with divisible projects, rank by:
quiz.why: PI measures NPV per rupee invested, which maximises total NPV from limited funds.

quiz.q: A certainty-equivalent coefficient of 0.7 on ₹50,000 gives:
quiz.why: Certain equivalent = 0.7 × 50,000 = ₹35,000.

questions.q: Interest on the loan used to finance a project is:
options: Ignored in cash flows; captured in the discount rate
questions.why: Financing cost is reflected in the cost of capital.

questions.q: (Revenue − cash costs) ₹4 lakh; depreciation ₹1 lakh; tax 30%. CFAT:
Cost ₹5 lakh; CFAT ₹2 lakh, ₹2 lakh, ₹3 lakh. Payback:
questions.why: ₹4 lakh after 2 years; ₹1 lakh of ₹3 lakh = 0.33 year.

questions.q: Average PAT ₹45,000; cost ₹3,00,000; salvage nil. ARR on average investment:
Cost ₹1,00,000; CFAT ₹40,000 for 3 years; PVAF(10%, 3) 2.4869. NPV:
PV of inflows ₹9 lakh; outlay ₹10 lakh. Decision:
questions.why: PI = 0.9 < 1 and NPV is negative.

questions.q: Ranking conflict between NPV and IRR is mainly due to:
questions.why: NPV assumes reinvestment at k, IRR at the IRR.

questions.q: Fisher's rate is the rate at which:
options: NPV profiles of two projects intersect
questions.why: At that rate both projects have equal NPV.

questions.q: Expected NPV: ₹6 lakh (0.4), ₹2 lakh (0.4), −₹5 lakh (0.2):
Budget ₹10 lakh; divisible projects A (cost 6, PI 1.3), B (cost 5, PI 1.2), C (cost 4, PI 1.1). Optimal choice:
questions.why: Rank by PI: A (₹6 lakh), then ₹4 lakh of B's ₹5 lakh = 80%.

questions.q: Certainty-equivalent analysis discounts at the risk-free rate because:
options: Risk has been removed from the cash flows
questions.why: Discounting at a risky rate would penalise risk twice.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Cost of Capital
courses.summary: Specific costs of debt, preference capital, equity and retained earnings; the dividend-growth and CAPM approaches; weighted average and marginal cost of capital; and value-based measures such as EVA.
outcomes: Compute after-tax cost of irredeemable and redeemable debt
Compute cost of preference capital
Estimate cost of equity by dividend-growth and CAPM approaches, including flotation costs
Compute WACC with book and market weights and marginal cost breaking points
Compute and interpret Economic Value Added

lessons.title: Cost of Debt and Preference Capital

scenes.text: A company issues 12% debentures at ₹96. The CFO notes that interest saves tax, so debt is cheaper than it looks.
Preference dividends, by contrast, come out of post-tax profit.

steps.title: Irredeemable debt
steps.body: Kd = I(1 − t)/NP, where I = annual interest, t = tax rate and NP = net proceeds (issue price − flotation costs). If issued at par with no costs, Kd = coupon rate × (1 − t).

steps.title: Redeemable debt (approximation)
steps.body: Kd = [I(1 − t) + (RV − NP)/n] ÷ [(RV + NP)/2], where RV = redemption value and n = years to maturity. The exact cost is the IRR of the after-tax cash flows.

steps.title: Worked example: redeemable
steps.body: 10% debentures, face ₹100, net proceeds ₹95, redeemable at par after 5 years, tax 30%. Kd = [10 × 0.7 + (100 − 95)/5] ÷ [(100 + 95)/2] = (7 + 1)/97.5 = 8.21%.

steps.title: Worked example: preference capital
steps.body: Irredeemable: dividend ₹9, NP ₹90 → Kp = 9/90 = 10%. Redeemable: dividend ₹10, RV ₹105, NP ₹95, n = 5 → Kp = [10 + (105 − 95)/5] ÷ [(105 + 95)/2] = 12/100 = 12%. No tax adjustment because preference dividend is not tax-deductible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Applying (1 − t) to preference dividends, or using face value instead of net proceeds when flotation costs exist.

activity.prompt: 11% debentures of ₹100 issued at ₹92 (net); irredeemable; tax 30%. Kd (%, two decimals)?

quiz.q: Debt is usually the cheapest source because:
options: It has no risk to the firm
It never has to be repaid
Interest is tax-deductible and lenders bear less risk
quiz.why: The tax shield lowers the effective cost, and lenders' prior claim means they demand a lower return.

quiz.q: 12% debt issued at par; tax 25%. Kd:
Preference dividend ₹8, net proceeds ₹100, irredeemable. Kp:
quiz.why: Kp = 8/100 = 8%, with no tax adjustment.

quiz.q: Redeemable debt: I(1 − t) = 7, (RV − NP)/n = 2, average = 100. Kd:

lessons.title: Cost of Equity and Retained Earnings

scenes.text: Equity has no fixed payment, so some think it is free. But shareholders expect a return or they sell, and the share price falls.
Two lenses: what dividends imply (Gordon) and what risk implies (CAPM).

steps.title: Dividend growth model
steps.body: Ke = D₁/P₀ + g, where D₁ = D₀(1 + g) is next year's dividend, P₀ = current market price and g = constant growth rate. For a new issue with flotation cost f: Ke = D₁/[P₀(1 − f)] + g.

steps.title: CAPM
steps.body: Ke = Rf + β(Rm − Rf). Rf = risk-free rate (e.g. yield on government securities), β = sensitivity of the share's return to market return, (Rm − Rf) = market risk premium.

steps.title: Retained earnings
steps.body: Retained earnings have an opportunity cost: shareholders could have invested the dividend elsewhere. Kr = Ke without flotation cost. If personal tax and brokerage are considered: Kr = Ke(1 − tp)(1 − b). Earnings–price approach: Ke = EPS/MPS (suits firms with no growth and full payout).

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: WACC formula
steps.body: WACC = Σ wᵢkᵢ = we·ke + wp·kp + wd·kd(1 − t). Weights may be book values (easy, stable) or market values (theoretically preferred, reflect current investor expectations), or target weights.

steps.title: Marginal cost of capital
steps.body: MCC is the cost of the next rupee raised. It rises at breaking points where a cheaper source is exhausted. Breaking point = Amount of the cheaper source available ÷ its weight. Example: retained earnings ₹20 lakh, equity weight 50% → beyond ₹40 lakh of new total capital, the firm must issue new equity at a higher cost.

steps.title: Project-specific rates
steps.body: WACC suits projects with the firm's average risk. For a riskier division, use a pure-play beta of comparable firms to build a divisional cost of capital.

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: EVA
steps.body: EVA = NOPAT − (WACC × Capital employed), where NOPAT = EBIT(1 − t). Positive EVA means the business earns more than the full cost of capital (debt and equity). Equivalent form: EVA = (ROCE − WACC) × Capital employed.

steps.title: Worked example

steps.title: MVA and shareholder wealth
steps.body: Market Value Added = Market value of the firm (equity + debt) − Capital employed. MVA equals the present value of expected future EVAs. The objective of financial management is wealth maximisation (maximising the market value of shares), which considers time value and risk, unlike profit maximisation.

steps.title: Worked example: MVA
steps.body: Market capitalisation ₹500 crore; debt ₹100 crore; capital employed ₹450 crore. MVA = 500 + 100 − 450 = ₹150 crore.

scenes.text: A Ludhiana cycle maker's sales rise 10%. Its EPS jumps 40%. Why so much?
Fixed operating costs and fixed interest magnify changes — that magnification is leverage.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: DOL = Contribution/EBIT = %ΔEBIT ÷ %ΔSales. DFL = EBIT/EBT = %ΔEPS ÷ %ΔEBIT (with preference dividend: EBIT/[EBT − Dp/(1 − t)]). DCL = DOL × DFL = Contribution/EBT = %ΔEPS ÷ %ΔSales.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
10,000 units at ₹50; variable cost ₹30/unit; fixed costs ₹1,20,000; interest ₹30,000.
Contribution = 10,000 × 20 = ₹2,00,000. EBIT = ₹80,000. EBT = ₹50,000.
DOL = 2,00,000/80,000 = 2.5. DFL = 80,000/50,000 = 1.6. DCL = 4.
Interpretation: a 10% rise in sales raises EBIT by 25% and EPS by 40%.

steps.title: Risk meaning
steps.body: DOL measures business risk (from fixed operating costs). DFL measures financial risk (from fixed financing charges). A firm with high DOL should usually keep DFL low, so that combined risk stays manageable.

steps.title: Worked example: operating break-even
steps.body: Break-even sales units = Fixed costs/Contribution per unit = 1,20,000/20 = 6,000 units. DOL becomes very large near break-even and falls as sales grow beyond it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using EBT in the DOL denominator, or forgetting to gross up preference dividend for tax in DFL.

scenes.text: A firm needs ₹20 lakh. Plan A: issue equity only. Plan B: half equity, half 10% debt.

steps.title: Indifference point
steps.body: (EBIT − I₁)(1 − t) − Dp ÷ N₁ = (EBIT − I₂)(1 − t) − Dp ÷ N₂. Solve for EBIT. Above this EBIT, the plan with more debt gives higher EPS; below it, the equity plan is better.

steps.title: Worked example: EPS at expected EBIT
steps.body: Expected EBIT ₹3,00,000. Plan A EPS = 2,25,000/2,00,000 = ₹1.125. Plan B EPS = 2,00,000 × 0.75/1,00,000 = ₹1.50. Plan B is better, but its financial break-even (EBIT = ₹1,00,000) is higher.

steps.title: Financial break-even
steps.body: EBIT at which EPS = 0: interest + preference dividend/(1 − t). Plan B: ₹1,00,000; Plan A: ₹0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Choosing purely by EPS. Higher EPS from debt comes with higher risk and may lower the P/E multiple, so share price need not rise.

steps.title: Net Income (NI) approach
steps.body: Durand: Kd and Ke are constant as debt rises. Since debt is cheaper, more debt lowers Ko and raises firm value. V = S + D, where S = (EBIT − I)/Ke.

steps.title: Net Operating Income (NOI) approach
steps.body: Ko and Kd are constant; Ke rises with leverage exactly to offset cheaper debt. V = EBIT/Ko, independent of structure; S = V − D.

steps.title: Traditional and MM
steps.body: Traditional view: moderate debt lowers Ko up to an optimum, then rising Ke and Kd raise it — an optimal capital structure exists. MM without taxes (1958): Proposition I — V is independent of capital structure; Proposition II — Ke = Ko + (Ko − Kd)D/S; maintained by arbitrage. MM with corporate taxes (1963): VL = VU + tD; value rises with debt due to the interest tax shield. Trade-off theory adds bankruptcy and agency costs; pecking-order theory says firms prefer internal funds, then debt, then equity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying MM (1958) claims debt is irrelevant to Ke — Proposition II says Ke rises with leverage; it is total value that is unaffected.

quiz.why: The present value of the perpetual interest tax shield is tD, which adds to the unlevered value.

quiz.why: Information asymmetry makes retained earnings the cheapest and least signalling source.

scenes.text: A mid-size pharma company in Hyderabad needs ₹300 crore for a new plant.

steps.title: Owners' funds
steps.body: Equity shares: permanent capital, no fixed charge, voting rights, highest cost. Issue routes: IPO/FPO, rights issue (to existing holders), bonus issue (capitalising reserves, no cash), private placement, preferential allotment and Qualified Institutions Placement (QIP) for listed companies. Retained earnings: internal, no flotation cost. Preference shares: fixed dividend, priority over equity; in India companies may issue only redeemable preference shares (maximum tenure 20 years, longer for infrastructure).

steps.title: Borrowed funds
steps.body: Debentures/bonds: secured or unsecured, convertible or non-convertible (NCDs), fixed coupon; interest tax-deductible. Term loans from banks and financial institutions: 3–10 years, with covenants. External Commercial Borrowings (ECB): foreign-currency loans under RBI's framework, carry exchange risk. Venture capital and private equity for start-ups and growth firms. Lease financing and hire purchase for assets.

steps.body: Market price ₹120 cum-rights; 1 new share for every 4 held at ₹95. Theoretical ex-rights price = (4 × 120 + 95)/5 = 575/5 = ₹115. Value of a right per existing share = (120 − 115) = ₹5.

steps.title: Choosing the mix
steps.body: Consider cost, risk (business risk and DOL), control (equity dilutes), flexibility, timing (market conditions), tax, and legal limits. Debt suits stable cash flows; equity suits volatile or early-stage firms.

lessons.title: Dividend Theories: Walter, Gordon and MM

scenes.text: A firm earns ₹10 per share and can reinvest at 15% while shareholders expect 10%.
Walter's model says: retain everything — the firm earns more than its shareholders could.

steps.title: Walter's model
steps.body: P = [D + (r/ke)(E − D)] ÷ ke, where E = EPS, D = DPS, r = internal rate of return, ke = cost of equity. Growth firm (r > ke): zero payout maximises P. Normal firm (r = ke): payout irrelevant. Declining firm (r < ke): 100% payout maximises P. Assumes all financing from retained earnings and constant r and ke.

steps.title: Gordon's model
steps.body: P = E(1 − b) ÷ (ke − br), where b = retention ratio and g = br. Similar conclusions to Walter's, and the 'bird-in-hand' argument: investors value near dividends more than uncertain future gains, so ke may rise with retention.

steps.title: MM irrelevance
steps.body: Under perfect markets, no taxes and given investment policy, dividend policy does not affect value. P₀ = (D₁ + P₁)/(1 + ke). Paying a dividend lowers the ex-dividend price by the same amount. Example: D₁ = ₹5, P₁ = ₹110, ke = 10% → P₀ = 115/1.10 = ₹104.55. If no dividend, P₁ = 104.55 × 1.10 = ₹115. Real-world factors (taxes, flotation costs, signalling, clientele) make dividends matter in practice; Lintner found firms smooth dividends toward a target payout.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using r/ke the wrong way round in Walter's formula, or forgetting the outer division by ke.

quiz.why: Shareholders can earn more than the firm, so distributing all earnings maximises price.

quiz.why: Gordon argued that investors prefer certain current dividends to uncertain future capital gains.

lessons.title: Operating Cycle and Working Capital Estimation

story.title: Cash tied up in the cycle

scenes.text: A garment exporter buys fabric, stitches, stores finished goods, sells on 45-day credit and collects.
Every day of that cycle needs financing — that is working capital.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: Gross working capital = current assets. Net working capital = current assets − current liabilities. Permanent (core) working capital is the minimum level always needed; temporary (fluctuating) working capital varies with seasons. Approaches to financing: matching (hedging), conservative (more long-term funds), aggressive (more short-term funds).

steps.title: Operating cycle
steps.body: Gross operating cycle = RM storage + WIP conversion + FG storage + debtors collection period. Net operating cycle (cash conversion cycle) = Gross − creditors payment period. RM days = Average RM stock/Daily RM consumption; Debtors days = Average debtors/Daily credit sales; and so on.

steps.title: Worked example: cycle
steps.body: RM 30 days; WIP 15 days; FG 20 days; debtors 45 days; creditors 40 days. Gross OC = 30 + 15 + 20 + 45 = 110 days. Net OC = 110 − 40 = 70 days. Number of cycles a year (360-day year) = 360/70 = 5.14.

steps.title: Worked example: estimation
steps.body:
Annual output 36,000 units (360 days). Cost per unit: material ₹50, labour ₹20, overheads ₹30; selling price ₹125. RM held 1 month; WIP ½ month (material full, labour and overheads 50%); FG 1 month; debtors 2 months (at cost); creditors 1 month; wages lag ½ month. Monthly output 3,000 units.
RM = 3,000 × 50 = 1,50,000. WIP = 1,500 × (50 + 10 + 15) = 1,12,500. FG = 3,000 × 100 = 3,00,000. Debtors = 6,000 × 100 = 6,00,000. Total CA = ₹11,62,500.
Creditors = 1,50,000; wages = 1,500 × 20 = 30,000. Net working capital = 11,62,500 − 1,80,000 = ₹9,82,500 (add contingency if specified).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Valuing debtors at selling price when the question asks for the cash-cost basis, or including depreciation in overhead cost for working capital.

story.title: Too much or too little cash

scenes.text: Holding idle cash loses interest; converting securities to cash too often costs brokerage.
Baumol applies the EOQ idea to cash.

steps.title: Motives and tools
steps.body: Keynes' motives: transaction, precautionary, speculative. Tools: cash budget (forecast receipts and payments), concentration banking, lock-box, electronic payments (RTGS/NEFT/UPI) to speed collections, and playing the float. Surplus cash is parked in liquid instruments such as treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit and liquid mutual funds.

steps.title: Baumol model
steps.body: Optimal cash withdrawal C* = √(2Tb/i), where T = total cash needed in the period, b = fixed cost per conversion, i = interest rate on securities. Total cost = (T/C)b + (C/2)i.

steps.title: Miller–Orr model
steps.body: For random cash flows: set a lower limit L, a return point Z = L + (3bσ²/4i)^(1/3), and an upper limit H = L + 3(Z − L). When cash hits H, buy securities to bring it back to Z; when it hits L, sell securities to restore Z. Here σ² is the daily variance of cash flows and i the daily interest rate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing an annual T with a daily interest rate in Baumol — keep periods consistent.

quiz.why: Precautionary balances cushion unforeseen outflows or delays in inflows.

scenes.text: A distributor can raise sales by ₹10 lakh by offering 60 days' credit instead of 30.
But it will tie up funds and face more bad debts. Is it worth it?

steps.title: Credit policy variables
steps.body: Credit standards (the 5 Cs: character, capacity, capital, collateral, conditions), credit period, cash discount, and collection effort. Evaluate a change by comparing incremental contribution with incremental costs: bad debts, collection costs, discount cost and the opportunity cost of extra investment in receivables (at cost of sales).

steps.title: Worked example: credit policy
steps.body: Extra sales ₹10,00,000; contribution 30% = ₹3,00,000. Bad debts 2% of extra sales = ₹20,000. Extra receivables at variable cost = 7,00,000 × 60/360 = ₹1,16,667; required return 15% → ₹17,500. Net benefit = 3,00,000 − 20,000 − 17,500 = ₹2,62,500 → adopt. (Here, for simplicity, the existing customers' collection period is assumed unchanged.)

steps.title: Inventory: EOQ and levels
steps.body: EOQ = √(2AO/C), where A = annual demand, O = ordering cost per order and C = carrying cost per unit per year. Reorder level = maximum usage × maximum lead time. Minimum level = ROL − (normal usage × normal lead time). Maximum level = ROL + EOQ − (minimum usage × minimum lead time). Safety stock guards against demand and lead-time uncertainty. ABC analysis focuses control on high-value items; JIT minimises stock.

steps.title: Worked example: EOQ
steps.body: A = 5,000 units; O = ₹400; C = ₹16. EOQ = √(2 × 5,000 × 400/16) = √2,50,000 = 500 units. Orders a year = 10. Ordering cost = 10 × 400 = ₹4,000; carrying cost = 500/2 × 16 = ₹4,000 (equal at EOQ). Total = ₹8,000.

steps.title: Worked example: reorder level
steps.body: Usage: max 400, normal 300, min 200 units a week. Lead time: max 6, normal 5, min 4 weeks. ROL = 400 × 6 = 2,400 units. Minimum level = 2,400 − 300 × 5 = 900. With EOQ 2,000: Maximum level = 2,400 + 2,000 − 200 × 4 = 3,600 units.

steps.title: Capital budgeting
steps.body: CFAT = (R − C)(1 − t) + tD. Payback = cost/annual CFAT. ARR = average PAT/average investment. NPV = Σ CFₜ/(1 + k)ᵗ − C₀. PI = PV inflows/PV outflows. IRR: NPV = 0; interpolate L + NPV_L/(NPV_L − NPV_H) × (H − L). Expected NPV = Σ p × NPV. CE: discount αCF at Rf.

steps.title: Cost of capital
steps.body: Kd (irredeemable) = I(1 − t)/NP. Kd (redeemable) = [I(1 − t) + (RV − NP)/n]/[(RV + NP)/2]. Kp = D/NP (no tax). Ke = D₁/P₀ + g; new issue D₁/[P₀(1 − f)] + g. CAPM: Rf + β(Rm − Rf). WACC = Σ wk. Breaking point = source available/weight. EVA = NOPAT − WACC × CE.

steps.title: Leverage and structure
steps.body: DOL = C/EBIT; DFL = EBIT/EBT; DCL = C/EBT. Indifference: (EBIT − I₁)(1 − t)/N₁ = (EBIT − I₂)(1 − t)/N₂. NI: S = NI/Ke, V = S + D. NOI: V = EBIT/Ko. MM II: Ke = Ko + (Ko − Kd)D/S. MM with tax: VL = VU + tD. TERP = (N × P + S)/(N + 1).

steps.title: Dividends and working capital
steps.body: Walter: P = [D + (r/ke)(E − D)]/ke. Gordon: P = E(1 − b)/(ke − br). MM: P₀ = (D₁ + P₁)/(1 + ke). Net OC = RM + WIP + FG + Debtors − Creditors days. Baumol C* = √(2Tb/i). EOQ = √(2AO/C). ROL = max usage × max lead time.

scenes.text: Sneha, an M.Com student, wants to study why small retailers in Jaipur adopt UPI.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: Research is a systematic, objective and replicable inquiry to discover facts, test theories or solve problems. Characteristics: systematic, logical, empirical, replicable, controlled, and critical. Kerlinger describes scientific research as systematic, controlled, empirical and critical investigation of hypothetical propositions.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: By purpose: basic (fundamental, theory-building) vs applied (solving a practical problem). By objective: descriptive (what is), analytical (why, using existing data), exploratory (clarify an unclear problem), explanatory/causal (cause–effect). By approach: quantitative (numbers, statistics) vs qualitative (meanings, interviews, themes); mixed methods combine both. By time: cross-sectional (one point) vs longitudinal (repeated over time). By setting: field, laboratory, desk research.

steps.title: Worked example: classifying studies
steps.body: 'Impact of GST on the working capital of MSMEs' — applied, causal, quantitative. 'Lived experience of women entrepreneurs' — qualitative, exploratory. 'Share of digital payments 2016–2025' — descriptive, longitudinal, secondary data.

steps.title: Inductive vs deductive
steps.body: Deductive: theory → hypothesis → data → confirmation (typical of quantitative studies). Inductive: observations → patterns → theory (typical of qualitative studies).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling any survey 'causal research' — surveys mostly describe and correlate; causation needs experimental or strong quasi-experimental designs.

steps.title: Research process
steps.body: 1. Identify and define the research problem. 2. Review literature. 3. Formulate objectives and hypotheses. 4. Prepare the research design. 5. Determine sample design. 6. Collect data. 7. Process and analyse data. 8. Test hypotheses. 9. Interpret and generalise. 10. Prepare the report.

steps.title: Problem and objectives
steps.body: A good problem is specific, researchable, significant, feasible (time, cost, data) and ethical. Objectives use action verbs: 'to examine', 'to compare', 'to identify the determinants of'. Variables: independent (cause), dependent (effect), moderating (changes the strength of a relationship), mediating (explains the mechanism), control (held constant).

steps.title: Hypotheses
steps.body: A hypothesis is a testable tentative statement about the relationship between variables. Null hypothesis H₀: no difference or no relationship. Alternative H₁: a difference or relationship exists; one-tailed (directional, e.g. 'greater than') or two-tailed (non-directional). Good hypotheses are clear, testable, specific, consistent with theory and stated before analysis.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Problem: low UPI use among small retailers. Objective: to examine the effect of perceived ease of use on UPI adoption. H₀: Perceived ease of use has no significant effect on UPI adoption. H₁: Perceived ease of use has a significant positive effect on UPI adoption (one-tailed). Independent: perceived ease of use; dependent: adoption; control: shop size.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Writing hypotheses that cannot be tested ('UPI is good for India') or stating the null as 'there is a relationship'.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: Research design is the blueprint for collecting, measuring and analysing data so that the research questions can be answered validly and economically. It specifies the type of study, sources, sampling, instruments, and analysis plan.

steps.title: Types of design
steps.body: Exploratory: flexible; literature search, expert interviews, focus groups, case studies. Descriptive: structured; cross-sectional surveys, panel studies; answers who, what, where, when, how much. Causal (experimental): manipulates an independent variable and controls other factors. Experimental designs: pre-experimental (one-shot case study; one-group pre-test/post-test), true experimental (pre-test/post-test control group with randomisation; post-test-only control group; Solomon four-group), quasi-experimental (no random assignment, e.g. time series, non-equivalent control group), and statistical designs (randomised block, Latin square, factorial).

steps.title: Validity
steps.body: Internal validity: did X really cause the change in Y? Threats: history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, selection, statistical regression, mortality (attrition). External validity: can results be generalised to other people, places and times? Randomisation and control groups protect internal validity; representative samples and realistic settings support external validity.

steps.title: Worked example: control group effect
steps.body: Training group: pre-test 60, post-test 72. Control: pre-test 58, post-test 63. Treatment effect = (72 − 60) − (63 − 58) = 12 − 5 = 7 points — the control group removes the effect of history and maturation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Attributing the entire pre–post change to the treatment in a one-group design; external events may explain part of it.

steps.title: Purpose
steps.body: A literature review shows what is known, identifies theories and methods used, avoids duplication, refines the problem and reveals the research gap. Sources: journals (Scopus/UGC-CARE-listed), books, theses (Shodhganga), working papers, reports (RBI, NSSO), databases (JSTOR, EBSCO, Google Scholar).

steps.title: Writing it
steps.body: Organise thematically or chronologically, not paper by paper. Synthesise: compare and contrast findings, methods and contexts. Evaluate quality. End with the gap: contextual (not studied in this region or sector), methodological (only cross-sectional studies exist), theoretical (a model not yet tested), or empirical (conflicting findings).

courses.summary: Population, sampling frame and sampling errors; probability and non-probability sampling; sample-size determination; levels of measurement; Likert, semantic differential and other scales; reliability (Cronbach's alpha) and validity; questionnaire design and primary versus secondary data.

steps.title: Key terms
steps.body: Population (universe): all units of interest. Sampling frame: the list from which the sample is drawn. Sampling unit and element. Parameter (population value) vs statistic (sample value). Sampling error: difference between statistic and parameter due to chance; non-sampling errors: frame errors, non-response, measurement and processing errors — these do not fall with sample size.

steps.title: Probability methods
steps.body: Simple random sampling: every unit has an equal chance (lottery, random numbers). Systematic: every kth unit after a random start, k = N/n. Stratified: divide into homogeneous strata and sample each (proportionate or disproportionate). Cluster: randomly select whole groups (e.g. villages), then survey all or some units in them. Multi-stage: sampling in stages (state → district → village → household).

steps.title: Worked example: proportionate stratified
steps.body: Branches: A 3,000, B 2,000, C 1,000 customers; sample 300 (5%). Allocation: A 150, B 100, C 50. Systematic alternative over a 5,000 list for 250: k = 20 — choose a random start between 1 and 20, then every 20th.

steps.title: Stratified vs cluster
steps.body: Strata are internally homogeneous and differ from each other; clusters are internally heterogeneous and similar to each other. Stratified improves precision; cluster reduces cost.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using systematic sampling on a list with a periodic pattern (e.g. every 10th flat is a corner flat), which biases the sample.

steps.title: Non-probability methods
steps.body: Convenience: whoever is available. Judgement (purposive): researcher selects informed units. Quota: fill quotas by characteristic (age, gender) non-randomly. Snowball: respondents refer others — useful for hard-to-reach groups. Results cannot be generalised with measurable sampling error.

steps.title: Sample size formulas
steps.body: For a mean: n = z²σ²/e². For a proportion: n = z²p(1 − p)/e². Use p = 0.5 when unknown (maximum variability). Finite population correction: n′ = n/[1 + (n − 1)/N]. z = 1.96 for 95%, 2.576 for 99%.

steps.title: Rules of thumb
steps.body: For regression, at least 10–20 observations per predictor; for SEM, often 200+. Always round sample size up and add allowance for non-response (e.g. divide by expected response rate).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Rounding sample size down, or using p = 0.5 and then claiming a larger margin of error than calculated.

quiz.q: If p is unknown, the safest value to use is:

quiz.q: Halving the margin of error roughly:
quiz.why: n is inversely proportional to e², so halving e multiplies n by four.

steps.title: Levels of measurement
steps.body: Nominal: categories without order (gender, bank name) — mode, chi-square. Ordinal: ordered ranks (ranking of brands) — median, rank correlation. Interval: equal intervals, no true zero (temperature °C, Likert summated scores often treated as interval) — mean, SD, t-test. Ratio: true zero (income, age, sales) — all statistics including ratios.

steps.title: Scales
steps.body: Comparative: paired comparison, rank order, constant sum. Non-comparative: graphic rating, itemised rating — Likert (strongly disagree to strongly agree, usually 5 or 7 points), semantic differential (bipolar adjectives such as modern–old-fashioned), Stapel (−5 to +5 single adjective). Thurstone and Guttman scales for attitude measurement.

steps.title: Reliability and validity
steps.body: Reliability = consistency: test–retest, parallel forms, split-half, internal consistency (Cronbach's α; ≥ 0.70 generally acceptable). α = [k/(k − 1)] × [1 − Σσᵢ²/σₜ²]. Validity = measuring what is intended: content (expert judgement), criterion (concurrent, predictive), construct (convergent and discriminant). A measure can be reliable without being valid, but not valid without being reliable.

steps.title: Worked example: Cronbach's alpha
steps.body: 5 items; sum of item variances 10; variance of total score 30. α = (5/4) × (1 − 10/30) = 1.25 × 0.667 = 0.83 → good internal consistency.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Computing a mean of nominal codes (e.g. 1 = male, 2 = female) and interpreting it.

quiz.q: Bipolar adjectives such as 'expensive–cheap' are used in a:

quiz.q: Cronbach's alpha measures:

quiz.q: A scale that correlates highly with measures of the same construct shows:

steps.title: Primary data methods
steps.body: Observation (participant/non-participant, structured/unstructured), interview (personal, telephone, depth), questionnaire (self-administered, online via Google Forms), schedule (filled by enumerator), focus groups, experiments.

steps.title: Questionnaire design steps
steps.body: 1. Specify information needed. 2. Choose method of administration. 3. Decide question content. 4. Choose response format (open-ended, dichotomous, multiple choice, scales). 5. Word questions clearly. 6. Sequence: easy and general first, sensitive and demographic last; use funnel approach and filter questions. 7. Layout and pre-coding. 8. Pilot test and revise.

steps.title: Wording pitfalls
steps.body: Avoid double-barrelled questions, leading questions ('Don't you agree…'), loaded words, jargon, ambiguous terms ('regularly'), double negatives and questions requiring memory far back.

steps.title: Secondary data

steps.title: Steps
steps.body: 1. State H₀ and H₁. 2. Choose significance level α (commonly 5%). 3. Select the test and compute the test statistic. 4. Find the critical value or p-value. 5. Decide: reject H₀ if |statistic| > critical value or p < α. 6. Interpret in plain language.

steps.title: Errors and p-value
steps.body: Type I error: rejecting a true H₀ (probability α). Type II error: failing to reject a false H₀ (probability β). Power = 1 − β. p-value: probability, assuming H₀ is true, of a result at least as extreme as observed. Critical z: two-tailed 1.96 (5%), 2.576 (1%); one-tailed 1.645 (5%), 2.33 (1%).

steps.title: Worked example: z for a mean
