steps.title: When to use t
steps.body: Use t when σ is unknown and estimated by s, especially for small samples (n < 30), assuming approximate normality. One-sample: t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n), df = n − 1. steps.title: Pearson's r
steps.body: r = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)/√[Σ(x − x̄)² Σ(y − ȳ)²]. Range −1 to +1. Measures linear association between interval/ratio variables. Significance: t = r√(n − 2)/√(1 − r²) with df = n − 2. Correlation does not imply causation.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
X (₹ lakh ads): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Y (₹ lakh sales): 2, 4, 5, 4, 5. x̄ = 3, ȳ = 4.
Σdxdy = 4 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 6; Σdx² = 10; Σdy² = 6.
r = 6/√60 = 0.775.
t = 0.775 × √3/√(1 − 0.6) = 1.342/0.632 = 2.12; critical t (df 3, 5%, two-tailed) = 3.182 → not significant with only 5 observations.

steps.title: Spearman's rank correlation
steps.body: ρ = 1 − 6Σd²/[n(n² − 1)], where d = difference in ranks. Used for ordinal data or non-linear monotonic relations. Example: n = 5; Σd² = 6 → ρ = 1 − 36/120 = 0.70. For tied ranks, assign average ranks and add correction factors.

steps.title: Interpreting strength

steps.title: One-way ANOVA
steps.body: H₀: all group means are equal. SST = SSB + SSW. SSB = Σ nⱼ(x̄ⱼ − x̄)²; SSW = ΣΣ(x − x̄ⱼ)². MSB = SSB/(k − 1); MSW = SSW/(N − k). F = MSB/MSW. Reject H₀ if F exceeds the critical F. Post-hoc tests (Tukey, Bonferroni) show which pairs differ. Two-way ANOVA adds a second factor and interaction.

steps.title: Multivariate techniques (overview)

Discriminant and logistic regression: predict group membership (default/no default). Conjoint analysis: trade-offs among product attributes. Structural equation modelling (SEM): test measurement and structural models together. Software: SPSS, R, Python, Stata, AMOS, SmartPLS.

steps.title: Why not many t-tests?
steps.body: With three groups, three t-tests at 5% each raise the chance of at least one false positive to about 14% (1 − 0.95³). ANOVA controls this overall error.

steps.title: Choosing a test
steps.body: One mean vs a value: z (σ known, large n) or one-sample t. Two independent means: independent t (Mann–Whitney if non-normal/ordinal). Two related means: paired t (Wilcoxon signed-rank). Three or more means: one-way ANOVA (Kruskal–Wallis). Two categorical variables: chi-square test of independence. Observed vs expected distribution: chi-square goodness of fit. Association of two interval variables: Pearson r; ordinal: Spearman ρ. Predicting Y from X(s): regression.

steps.title: Sampling and measurement
steps.body: k = N/n. Proportionate stratum size = (Nₕ/N) × n. n = z²σ²/e²; n = z²p(1 − p)/e²; n′ = n/[1 + (n − 1)/N]. α = [k/(k − 1)][1 − Σσᵢ²/σₜ²]. s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1).

steps.body: z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n); z (proportion) = (p̂ − p₀)/√[p₀(1 − p₀)/n]. t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n). Paired t = d̄/(s_d/√n). χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E; E = RT × CT/N; df = (r − 1)(c − 1). F = MSB/MSW.

steps.title: Expected and χ²

steps.title: Investment vs speculation
steps.body: Investment: commitment of funds for a reasonable return with moderate risk over a longer horizon, based on fundamental analysis. steps.title: Market structure

Market infrastructure: clearing corporations (NSE Clearing, Indian Clearing Corporation) guarantee settlement; depositories (NSDL, CDSL) hold securities in dematerialised form; depository participants and brokers serve investors. Indian equities settle on T+1.

steps.title: Regulator

Unsystematic (specific, diversifiable) risk comes from firm or industry factors: strikes, management, product failure — reduced by diversification. Total risk = systematic + unsystematic (in variance terms).

steps.title: Bond price

steps.title: Premises
steps.body: Prices discount everything; prices move in trends; history repeats because of crowd psychology. Technical analysis studies price and volume, not intrinsic value.

steps.title: Dow theory
steps.body: Three movements: primary trend (months to years), secondary reactions (weeks to months), daily fluctuations. Primary bull market: higher highs and higher lows; bear: lower highs and lower lows. Averages must confirm each other; volume confirms trend. Elliott wave theory extends this with five-wave impulses and three-wave corrections.

steps.title: Charts and patterns

steps.title: Three forms
steps.body: Weak form: prices reflect all past price and volume information → technical analysis cannot earn abnormal returns. Tests: serial correlation, runs tests, filter rules. Semi-strong form: prices reflect all public information → fundamental analysis of public data cannot earn abnormal returns. Tests: event studies (earnings, splits, bonuses). Strong form: prices reflect all information, public and private → even insiders cannot earn abnormal returns; generally rejected, which is why insider trading is prohibited (SEBI PIT Regulations).

steps.title: Random walk
steps.body: In a weak-form efficient market, successive price changes are independent — prices follow a random walk. This does not mean prices are irrational; it means new information arrives randomly.

steps.title: Anomalies and behavioural finance
steps.body: Documented anomalies: January effect, size effect, value (low P/B) effect, momentum, post-earnings-announcement drift. Behavioural finance explains them with biases: overconfidence, herding, loss aversion, anchoring, disposition effect.

steps.title: Implications
steps.body: For most investors in efficient markets: low-cost passive investing (index funds, ETFs), diversification, and focusing on asset allocation.

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: Assumptions and frontier
steps.body: Markowitz (1952): investors are risk-averse, care about mean and variance, and prefer higher return for given risk and lower risk for given return. The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios that dominate all others. The global minimum-variance portfolio is its leftmost point. The optimal portfolio is where the investor's highest indifference curve touches the frontier.

steps.title: Diversification in numbers
steps.body: For an equally weighted portfolio of n stocks: σp² = (1/n)·average variance + (1 − 1/n)·average covariance. As n grows, the first term vanishes and risk approaches the average covariance — the market (systematic) risk that cannot be diversified away.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Average variance 900; average covariance 200. n = 10: σp² = 90 + 0.9 × 200 = 270 → σp = 16.4%. n = 50: 18 + 196 = 214 → σp = 14.6%. As n → ∞: σp² → 200 → σp = 14.1%.

steps.title: Inputs problem
steps.body: With n assets, Markowitz needs n returns, n variances and n(n − 1)/2 covariances — for 100 stocks, 4,950 covariances. Sharpe's single-index model reduces this burden.

steps.title: Capital market line
steps.body: With risk-free lending and borrowing, efficient portfolios lie on the CML: E(Rp) = Rf + [(E(Rm) − Rf)/σm]·σp. The slope is the market price of risk per unit of total risk. Example: Rf 6%, E(Rm) 14%, σm 20%: a portfolio with σp 15% should return 6 + 0.4 × 15 = 12%.

steps.title: Security market line (CAPM)
steps.body: E(Ri) = Rf + βi[E(Rm) − Rf], with βi = Cov(i, m)/σm². Applies to all securities and portfolios, efficient or not. Securities plotting above the SML are undervalued (positive alpha); below it, overvalued.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Rf 6%; E(Rm) 13%; β 1.3. Required return = 6 + 1.3 × 7 = 15.1%. Analyst's forecast 17% → alpha = +1.9% → undervalued, buy.
Beta estimation: Cov(i, m) = 48; σm² = 40 → β = 1.2.

steps.title: Assumptions and critique
steps.body: Single-period, mean–variance investors with homogeneous expectations; unlimited borrowing and lending at Rf; no taxes or transaction costs; all assets marketable. Critiques: Roll's critique (true market portfolio unobservable), empirical SML flatter than predicted, and factors such as size and value explain returns (Fama–French).

scenes.text: Fund A returned 15%, Fund B 13%. A looks better — but A took far more risk.
Risk-adjusted measures compare reward per unit of risk.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Sharpe ratio = (Rp − Rf)/σp — reward per unit of total risk; suits evaluating an investor's whole portfolio. Treynor ratio = (Rp − Rf)/βp — reward per unit of systematic risk; suits a well-diversified portfolio that is part of a larger holding. Jensen's alpha = Rp − [Rf + βp(Rm − Rf)] — return above CAPM required return. Information ratio = active return/tracking error.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Fund: Rp 15%, σ 18%, β 1.2. Market: 12%, σ 15%. Rf 6%.
Sharpe: fund (15 − 6)/18 = 0.50; market 6/15 = 0.40 → fund better.
Treynor: fund 9/1.2 = 7.5; market 6/1 = 6 → fund better.
Jensen: 15 − (6 + 1.2 × 6) = 15 − 13.2 = +1.8% → positive alpha.

steps.title: When rankings differ
steps.body: A fund can rank high on Treynor but low on Sharpe if it is poorly diversified — it carries a lot of unsystematic risk that Treynor ignores. The difference between rankings signals diversification quality.

steps.title: M² measure
steps.body: Modigliani's M² = Rf + Sharpe × σm, i.e. the fund's return if levered to market risk. Fund above: 6 + 0.5 × 15 = 13.5% vs market 12% → outperforms by 1.5%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Comparing Sharpe ratios of a fund and a market computed over different periods, or forgetting to subtract Rf.

lessons.title: Futures and Options: Payoffs and Hedging

scenes.text: A fund manager fears a market fall before the Union Budget.
Buying Nifty puts or selling Nifty futures can hedge the portfolio.

steps.title: Instruments
steps.body: Forward: OTC, customised. Futures: exchange-traded, standardised, marked to market daily with margins. Options: right but not obligation — call (buy) or put (sell) at strike K; buyer pays a premium; European (exercise at expiry) or American (any time). Indian index options are European; stock F&O in India are physically settled.

steps.title: Payoffs at expiry
steps.body: Long call: max(ST − K, 0) − premium. Long put: max(K − ST, 0) − premium. Short positions are mirror images. Long futures: ST − F; short futures: F − ST. Call break-even = K + premium; put break-even = K − premium.

steps.title: Worked example: payoffs
steps.body:
Call K ₹500, premium ₹20, ST ₹540 → profit 40 − 20 = ₹20. ST ₹490 → loss = premium ₹20.
Put K ₹500, premium ₹15, ST ₹470 → profit 30 − 15 = ₹15.

steps.title: Worked example: cost of carry
steps.body: Spot ₹1,000; risk-free 8% continuously compounded; 3 months; no dividends. F = S·e^(rt) = 1,000 × e^(0.02) = ₹1,020.20. If the futures trades at ₹1,035, cash-and-carry arbitrage: buy spot, sell futures, earn ≈ ₹14.80 risk-free.

steps.title: Hedging
steps.body: Number of futures contracts to hedge = (Portfolio value × β)/(Futures price × lot size). Example: portfolio ₹1.2 crore, β 1.25, Nifty futures 24,000, lot 25 → 1,50,00,000/6,00,000 = 25 contracts sold.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the premium when computing option profit, or confusing the payoff (before premium) with profit.

steps.title: Put–call parity (European, no dividends)
steps.body: C + PV(K) = P + S₀. With discrete annual compounding PV(K) = K/(1 + r)ᵗ; with continuous, K·e^(−rt). Violations allow arbitrage.

steps.title: One-step binomial
steps.body: Up factor u, down factor d, risk-free growth R = 1 + r per period. Risk-neutral probability p = (R − d)/(u − d). Option value = [p·Cu + (1 − p)·Cd]/R. Requires d < R < u.

steps.title: Black–Scholes inputs
steps.body: Spot price, strike, time to expiry, risk-free rate, volatility (and dividends). Call value rises with S, T, σ and r; falls with K. Greeks: delta, gamma, theta, vega, rho.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the real-world probability of an up move instead of the risk-neutral p, or forgetting to discount the expected payoff.

steps.title: Return, risk, bonds
steps.body: HPR = (D + P₁ − P₀)/P₀. E(R) = Σ pR. σ² = Σ p(R − E)². CV = σ/E. Bond P = Σ C/(1 + y)ᵗ + F/(1 + y)ⁿ. YTM ≈ [C + (F − P)/n]/[(F + P)/2]. Current yield = C/P. D_mod = D_Mac/(1 + y); ΔP/P ≈ −D_mod × Δy.

steps.title: Equity
steps.body: P₀ = D₁/(k − g). Two-stage: PV of high-growth dividends + Pₙ/(1 + k)ⁿ with Pₙ = Dₙ₊₁/(k − g). Justified P/E = payout/(k − g). ROE = margin × turnover × equity multiplier. RSI = 100 − 100/(1 + RS).

steps.title: Portfolio
steps.body: E(Rp) = Σ wE. σp² = wA²σA² + wB²σB² + 2wAwBρσAσB. Min-variance wA = (σB² − Cov)/(σA² + σB² − 2Cov). CML: Rf + [(Rm − Rf)/σm]σp. SML: Rf + β(Rm − Rf). β = Cov(i, m)/σm². σi² = β²σm² + σ²(e). APT: Rf + Σ bλ.

steps.title: Performance and derivatives
steps.body: Sharpe = (Rp − Rf)/σ; Treynor = (Rp − Rf)/β; Jensen α = Rp − [Rf + β(Rm − Rf)]; M² = Rf + Sharpe × σm. NAV = (assets − liabilities)/units. F = S·e^(rt). Call profit = max(S − K, 0) − c; put = max(K − S, 0) − p. Parity: C + PV(K) = P + S. Binomial p = (R − d)/(u − d).

lessons.title: Lab: Estimating Beta from Return Data

scenes.text: You have five periods of returns for a stock and the Nifty.
Compute covariance and variance to get beta and alpha — the characteristic line.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
Deviations stock: 4, 0, −8, 8, −4. Market: 4, 0, −6, 6, −4.
Σ(product) = 16 + 0 + 48 + 48 + 16 = 128.
Σ(market dev²) = 16 + 0 + 36 + 36 + 16 = 104.
β = 128/104 = 1.23 (the n − 1 terms cancel).
α = 6 − 1.23 × 4 = 1.08%. Characteristic line: Rs = 1.08 + 1.23 Rm.

steps.title: Using beta
steps.body: With Rf 5% and expected market return 11%, required return = 5 + 1.23 × 6 = 12.38%.

steps.title: Viva
steps.body: Why does n − 1 cancel? Both covariance and variance divide by it. What does β > 1 mean? The stock is more volatile than the market (aggressive). What is R²? The share of the stock's variance explained by the market.
